questions.stem: A 55-year-old male patient is being treated for peptic ulcer disease and presents with symptoms of breast tenderness and decreased libido. His current medication includes an H2 blocker. Which of the following H2 blockers is most likely responsible for these antiandrogenic effects?
questions.stemHtml: A 55-year-old male patient is being treated for peptic ulcer disease and presents with symptoms of breast tenderness and decreased libido. His current medication includes an H2 blocker. Which of the following H2 blockers is most likely responsible for these antiandrogenic effects?
questions.solution: > Cimetidine is an H2 receptor antagonist that reduces gastric acid secretion in conditions such as peptic ulcer disease and GERD. Cimetidine is known for its antiandrogenic effects, including gynecomastia, breast tenderness, and decreased libido, due to its ability to inhibit estradiol metabolism and displace dihydrotestosterone from its receptor. Ranitidine (Option A): It has no significant antiandrogenic effects and is generally well-tolerated, with a lower risk of CNS effects and fewer drug interactions compared to cimetidine. Famotidine (Option B): It also lacks significant antiandrogenic effects and has minimal drug interactions. It is more potent and has a longer action duration than ranitidine and cimetidine. Nizatidine (Option D): It has no significant antiandrogenic effects and minimal drug interactions, with a similar efficacy and side effect profile to ranitidine, although it is used less frequently. @Neet_pg_bot

Bezold-Jarisch reflex or coronary chemoreflex: Activators : Capsaicin, serotonin, phenylbiguanide, veratridine and pathophysiologic conditions like reperfusion after myocardial ischemia ( increased production of oxygen radicals and agents used as radio contrast for coronary angiography). Mechanism: Activation of chemosensitive vagal C fibers (Option C) in the cardiopulmonary region (juxtacapillary region of alveoli, ventricles, atria, great veins, and pulmonary artery). questions.stemHtml: A patient is undergoing an endoscopy for epigastric pain. The report shows a giant duodenal ulcer in the duodenal cap, and a second one is noted in the second part of the duodenum. Which investigation should be done next in this patient?
questions.solution: Correct answer is A: Secretin study Secretin study is indicated to diagnose Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, which can present with multiple or giant duodenal ulcers due to excessive gastric acid secretion. It entails fasting gastrin levels and then levels few minutes after secretin injection. Breath urea test only detects H. pylori infection, not causes of multiple/giant ulcers. Somatostatin scintigraphy identifies neuroendocrine tumors but is not diagnostic for acid hypersecretion. Endoscopic ultrasound visualizes lesions but does not assess gastric secretory function. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solutionHtml:
p> 

Explanation:

Receptor potential is the graded depolarizing potential in a sensory receptor in response to a stimulus. Its magnitude varies with the intensity of the stimulus.

 

Receptor Potentials

  • A receptor potential is a type of graded potential that occurs in sensory receptors. It is a local, non-propagated change in membrane potential that occurs in response to a stimulus.
  • Receptor potential is not an action potential; instead, it causes the sensory neuron to fire action potentials.
  • Once the receptor potential reaches a critical threshold, it triggers an action potential at the sensory nerve's first node of Ranvier.

Receptor Potential" data-author="NA" data-hash="7858" data-license="NA" data-source="NA" data-tags="April2025" height="430" src="https://image.prepladder.com/notes/4dckPzu4YYs0VLdSl2ED1744015597.png" width="500" />

Factors affecting receptor potential:

  • Proportional Response: Amplitude of receptor potential is generally proportional to stimulus intensity.
  • Nature: Non-propagated, depolarizing potential in sensory receptors.
  • Threshold: When it reaches a critical level, an action potential is generated.
  • Stimulus Intensity: Stronger stimuli lead to larger receptor potentials.

 

Mechanism of receptor potential generation in Pacinian Corpuscle

 


 

 

Pacinian Corpuscle Mechanism

Mechanical Stimulation

  • Pressure deforms lamellae surrounding sensory nerve ending.

Ion Channels

  • Deformation opens mechanically-gated ion channels, mainly sodium (Na+).

Sodium Influx

  • Rapid influx of Na+ generates the receptor potential.

Graded Response

  • Larger deformation (stronger stimulus) leads to a larger receptor potential.

Action Potential

  • If the potential reaches ~10 mV, an action potential is generated at the first Node of Ranvier.

 

sensory nerve fiber" data-author="NA" data-hash="7859" data-license="NA" data-source="NA" data-tags="April2025" height="358" src="https://image.prepladder.com/notes/RwU5xVtZreVvDRUsznng1744015663.png" width="500" />

Action potential (Option A) is an all-or-none electrical signal that occurs after the receptor potential reaches a threshold. 

Synaptic potential (Option C) occurs at synapses between neurons, not in sensory receptors. 

Resting potential (Option D) is the baseline electrical state of a cell when it is not stimulated.

options.label: B

options.label: D

questions.solution: Serum progesterone should be >3ng/ml on day 21 to suggest ovulation , and any value below 3ng/ml does not suggest ovulation. Progesterone levels rise to 4-6 ng/mL during ovulation as the corpus luteum forms after the egg is released. During the luteal phase , progesterone levels range from approximately 5 to 20 ng/mL. Serial follicular monitoring is done from the start of day 9 to assess the increase in follicle size from 15mm to 20mm. Serial follicular monitoring where follicle size increases from 15mm to 20mm (Option B): Serial follicular monitoring is done by transvaginal ultrasonography > transabdominal sonography. It indicates ovulation when the follicle size increases from 15mm to 20mm and then shrinks. Serum LH = 40mIU/ml (Option C): Serum LH levels in the range of 35-50 mIU/ml indicate that ovulation has occurred. Diagnostic laparoscopy showed a yellow punctum on the ovary (Option D) indicates the presence of corpus luteum, which signifies that ovulation has occurred. @Neet_pg_bot

• Serum progesterone should be >3ng/ml on day 21 to suggest ovulation, and any value below 3ng/ml does not suggest ovulation.

 

  • Progesterone levels rise to 4-6 ng/mL during ovulation as the corpus luteum forms after the egg is released. During the luteal phase, progesterone levels range from approximately 5 to 20 ng/mL.
  • Serial follicular monitoring is done from the start of day 9 to assess the increase in follicle size from 15mm to 20mm.

Serial follicular monitoring where follicle size increases from 15mm to 20mm (Option B): Serial follicular monitoring is done by transvaginal ultrasonography > transabdominal sonography. It indicates ovulation when the follicle size increases from 15mm to 20mm and then shrinks.

Serum LH = 40mIU/ml (Option C): Serum LH levels in the range of 35-50 mIU/ml indicate that ovulation has occurred.

Diagnostic laparoscopy showed a yellow punctum on the ovary (Option D) indicates the presence of corpus luteum, which signifies that ovulation has occurred.

questions.answerText: The arrangement of melanosomes influences skin pigmentation.
questions.solution: > Size of melanosomes influences their arrangement within keratinocytes, which in turn affects skin pigmentation. Larger melanosomes, observed in darker skin tones, are typically dispersed individually. Melanin Types and Production: Two main types: Eumelanin : Brownish-black, responsible for darker skin tones. Pheomelanin : Orangish-red, found in lighter skin tones. Synthesis process (Melanogenesis): Melanosomes : Melanin is stored within specialized organelles called melanosomes, which are produced by melanocytes. Size and Distribution: Darker skin: Larger melanosomes (Option A) Lighter skin: Smaller melanosomes (Option B) Degradation: (Option C) Varies between skin types. Lighter skin: Melanosome complexes show degradative changes due to lysosomal enzymes. Darker skin: Larger melanosomes can remain intact up to the stratum corneum. Melanin and Skin Color: Key factors: Type of melanin, Melanosome size, Melanosome distribution (dispersed vs. aggregated), Skin color is NOT solely determined by the number of melanocytes.   • Two main types:
    • Eumelanin: Brownish-black, responsible for darker skin tones.
    • Pheomelanin: Orangish-red, found in lighter skin tones.
  • Synthesis process (Melanogenesis):

 

  • Melanosomes:
    • Melanin is stored within specialized organelles called melanosomes, which are produced by melanocytes.
    • Size and Distribution:
      • Darker skin: Larger melanosomes (Option A)
      • Lighter skin: Smaller melanosomes (Option B)
    • Degradation: (Option C)

      • Darker skin: Larger melanosomes can remain intact up to the stratum corneum.

    • Key factors: Type of melanin, Melanosome size, Melanosome distribution (dispersed vs. aggregated),
    • Skin color is NOT solely determined by the number of melanocytes.

    • UV radiation
    • Hormones: Estrogens - increase pigmentation; Melanocortins - melanin production.

Platelets

General Description

Small, granulated, non-nucleated discs important for hemostasis

Size

1-4 µm in diameter

Concentration in Blood

150,000 - 450,000/µL

Half-life

~4 days

Origin

Formed from megakaryocytes in the bone marrow

Distribution

60-75% in circulation; the remainder mainly in the spleen

Splenectomy Effect

Causes an increase in platelet count (thrombocytosis) (Option B)

Thrombopoietin

Produced by liver and kidneys; regulates platelet production (Option D)

Membrane Receptors

For collagen, ADP, von Willebrand factor and fibrinogen

Cytoplasmic Components

Actin, myosin, glycogen, lysosomes and granules

Granules

Adhere to exposed collagen and von Willebrand factor; release granule contents upon activation

Deficiency Effect

Thrombocytopenic purpura (easy bruising, multiple subcutaneous hemorrhages)

Interleukins

IL-1, IL-3, IL-6, IL-11 stimulate platelet production (Option C)

Inflammation, thrombopoietin and IL-1, IL-3, IL-6, IL-11

Osteoid osteoma (Option B): A benign tumour usually presenting with localised pain, commonly relieved by NSAIDs, and a radiologically distinct nidus.

Chronic osteomyelitis (Option D): Typically presents with suppuration (pus formation) and often abscess formation, which is absent in this case.

options.label: A
options.text: Drains to submental nodes; level I neck dissection is sufficient.

options.label: B
options.text: Drains to ipsilateral submandibular nodes; levels I-III neck dissection is recommended.

options.label: C
options.text: High risk of contralateral metastasis; bilateral neck dissection is needed.

options.label: D
options.text: Drains to preauricular and parotid nodes; requires superficial parotidectomy.

questions.answerText: Drains to ipsilateral submandibular nodes; levels I-III neck dissection is recommended.
questions.solution: Explanation: The lymphatic drainage of the lower lip is primarily to the submental (level IA) and submandibular (level IB) nodes . There's a significant risk of occult nodal metastasis for a lesion of this size, especially one close to the commissure. Therefore, a selective neck dissection, including levels I-III on the ipsilateral side, is typically recommended even in N0. Management 1. Early Stage (T1-T2N0): Wide local excision with 1 cm margins Consider elective neck dissection for tumors >2 cm or >4 mm depth Reconstruction: Primary closure, local flaps, or skin grafts 2. Advanced Stage (T3-T4 or N+): Wide local excision with ≥1 cm margins Neck dissection (comprehensive or selective based on nodal status) Complex reconstruction (local/regional flaps, free tissue transfer) Adjuvant radiotherapy or chemoradiotherapy based on pathological findings 3. Management of the Neck: Elective neck dissection for high-risk tumors (>2 cm, >4 mm depth) Therapeutic neck dissection for clinically positive nodes Levels typically addressed: I-III for N0 neck, I-V for N+ neck @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Explanation:

  • The lymphatic drainage of the lower lip is primarily to the submental (level IA) and submandibular (level IB) nodes.
  • There's a significant risk of occult nodal metastasis for a lesion of this size, especially one close to the commissure.
  • Therefore, a selective neck dissection, including levels I-III on the ipsilateral side, is typically recommended even in N0.

 

 

 

Management

1. Early Stage (T1-T2N0):

  • Wide local excision with 1 cm margins
  • Consider elective neck dissection for tumors >2 cm or >4 mm depth
  • Reconstruction: Primary closure, local flaps, or skin grafts

 

2. Advanced Stage (T3-T4 or N+):

  • Wide local excision with ≥1 cm margins
  • Neck dissection (comprehensive or selective based on nodal status)
  • Complex reconstruction (local/regional flaps, free tissue transfer)
  • Adjuvant radiotherapy or chemoradiotherapy based on pathological findings
 

3. Management of the Neck:

  • Elective neck dissection for high-risk tumors (>2 cm, >4 mm depth)
  • Therapeutic neck dissection for clinically positive nodes
  • Levels typically addressed: I-III for N0 neck, I-V for N+ neck

The genetic mutation commonly associated with achondroplasia is in the FGFR3 gene. Achondroplasia is usually diagnosed through physical examination and confirmed with genetic testing to identify mutations in the FGFR3 gene. Management focuses on addressing associated health issues and improving quality of life. This includes regular monitoring for complications like spinal problems or ear infections, physical therapy to enhance mobility and strength, and sometimes surgical interventions to address skeletal deformities. questions.stemHtml: A 30 year old woman, G2P1, presents in active labour at 40 weeks of gestation. Examination reveals the fetus is malpositioned at an occiput posterior position. If the fetus has a flexed neck and is of normal size, the maternal pelvis is adequate and has strong uterine contractions. What is the most likely outcome of the labour?
questions.solution: le conditions, the occiput posterior (OP) position usually progresses to normal labour and results in a normal vaginal delivery. Strong uterine contractions promote good flexion of the fetal neck, aiding in the descent of the fetus. The fetal head undergoes an internal rotation by 3/8th of a circle, positioning the occiput behind the pubic symphysis. Shoulders rotate by 2/8th of a circle to occupy the oblique diameter. The fetus descends further down in the pelvis, similar to the occiput anterior (OA) position. Head restitutes by 1/8th of a circle in the opposite direction of the internal rotation. The delivery process then proceeds like a normal vaginal delivery in the occiput anterior position. Occipitosacral arrest ( Option A) occurs when the fetal occiput mal-rotates posteriorly towards the sacral hollow. Although spontaneous delivery can sometimes happen in this position, if labour stops progressing, it is termed occipitosacral arrest. Deep transverse arrest (Option C) occurs when the occiput rotates 1/8th of a circle anteriorly, causing the sagittal suture to lie in the oblique diameter of the pelvis and then become arrested in that position. DTA seen in android >> anthropoid Oblique posterior arrest (Option D) due to nonrotation occurs when the sinciput and occiput simultaneously contact the pelvic floor because of fetal head deflexion. This results in the sagittal suture lying in the bispinous diameter of the pelvis, leading to arrest in that position. @Neet_pg_bot

  • Head restitutes by 1/8th of a circle in the opposite direction of the internal rotation.
  • The delivery process then proceeds like a normal vaginal delivery in the occiput anterior position.

Occipitosacral arrest (Option A) occurs when the fetal occiput mal-rotates posteriorly towards the sacral hollow. Although spontaneous delivery can sometimes happen in this position, if labour stops progressing, it is termed occipitosacral arrest.

On examination, her intraocular pressure (IOP) is elevated, and a cup-to-disc ratio of 0.7 is noted in both eyes. She is prescribed a prostaglandin analog as first-line therapy. questions.solution: on: Anti-Glaucoma Drugs: 1. Prostaglandin F2α Agonists (Option C) Examples: Latanoprost, Bimatoprost, Travoprost, Tafluprost Mechanism: Increases uveoscleral outflow Uses: First-line for primary open-angle and angle-closure glaucoma Side Effects: Sandy eyes, orbital fat atrophy, anterior uveitis, cystoid macular edema, heterochromia iridis, hypertrichosis Contraindications: Cystoid macular edema, diabetes mellitus 2. Beta Blockers (Option D) Non-Selective: Timolol, Levobunolol, Carteolol, Metipranolol More effective but contraindicated in asthma Selective: Betaxolol (retinoprotective), Levobetaxolol Safer in asthma Mechanism: Reduces aqueous secretion from ciliary epithelium Side Effects: Allergic blepharoconjunctivitis, dry eyes, corneal hypoesthesia 3. Alpha-2 Agonists (Option A) Examples: Brimonidine (long-term use), Apraclonidine (IOP spikes) Mechanism: Reduces aqueous production, increases uveoscleral outflow Side Effects: Lid retraction, respiratory depression (Brimonidine), allergic blepharoconjunctivitis Contraindications: Children <2 years Brimonidine: Safest during pregnancy (Category B) 4. Miotics (Option B) Examples: Pilocarpine, Physostigmine, Echothiophate Mechanism: Stimulates M3 receptors, increasing trabecular outflow Side Effects: Brow pain, miosis, cataract (Echothiophate), retinal tears 5. Carbonic Anhydrase Inhibitors Examples: Acetazolamide (systemic), Brinzolamide, Dorzolamide (topical) Mechanism: Inhibits aqueous secretion from ciliary epithelium Uses: Acute congestive glaucoma (with IV mannitol) Side Effects: Ciliary edema, secondary angle-closure glaucoma (Topiramate, Zonisamide) 6. questions.solutionHtml:
on:

 

Anti-Glaucoma Drugs:

1. Prostaglandin F2α Agonists (Option C)

  • Examples: Latanoprost, Bimatoprost, Travoprost, Tafluprost
  • Mechanism: Increases uveoscleral outflow
  • Uses: First-line for primary open-angle and angle-closure glaucoma
  • Side Effects: Sandy eyes, orbital fat atrophy, anterior uveitis, cystoid macular edema, heterochromia iridis, hypertrichosis
  • Contraindications: Cystoid macular edema, diabetes mellitus

 

2. Beta Blockers (Option D)

  • Non-Selective: Timolol, Levobunolol, Carteolol, Metipranolol
    • More effective but contraindicated in asthma
  • Selective: Betaxolol (retinoprotective), Levobetaxolol
    • Safer in asthma
  • Mechanism: Reduces aqueous secretion from ciliary epithelium
  • Side Effects: Allergic blepharoconjunctivitis, dry eyes, corneal hypoesthesia

 

3. Alpha-2 Agonists (Option A)

  • Examples: Brimonidine (long-term use), Apraclonidine (IOP spikes)
  • Mechanism: Reduces aqueous production, increases uveoscleral outflow
  • Side Effects: Lid retraction, respiratory depression (Brimonidine), allergic blepharoconjunctivitis
  • Contraindications: Children <2 years
  • Brimonidine: Safest during pregnancy (Category B)

 

4. Miotics (Option B)

  • Examples: Pilocarpine, Physostigmine, Echothiophate
  • Mechanism: Stimulates M3 receptors, increasing trabecular outflow
  • Side Effects: Brow pain, miosis, cataract (Echothiophate), retinal tears

 

5. Carbonic Anhydrase Inhibitors

  • Examples: Acetazolamide (systemic), Brinzolamide, Dorzolamide (topical)
  • Mechanism: Inhibits aqueous secretion from ciliary epithelium
  • Uses: Acute congestive glaucoma (with IV mannitol)
  • Side Effects: Ciliary edema, secondary angle-closure glaucoma (Topiramate, Zonisamide)

 

6. Newer Drugs

  • Netarsudil (Rho kinase inhibitor): Increases trabecular outflow; Side effect - vortex keratopathy
  • Omidenepag (PGE2 agonist): Increases both trabecular and uveoscleral outflow

questions.solution: roductive systems are those that share a common embryologic origin despite their different functions in adulthood. Though very useful when intervention is required, ERCP is not considered a non-invasive technique, making it less appropriate. questions.solution: ong>Explanation: Filarial infection is the most common cause of chyluria, as it can obstruct intestinal lymphatics, leading to lymph leakage into the urine. Chyluria Passage of milky white chylous urine, aggravated after fatty meals. Causes: Most Common: Filarial infections (2% of cases). Other Causes: Tumors, tuberculosis, malaria, and ascariasis infestation. Mechanism: Obstruction of intestinal lymphatic vessels leads to high lymphatic pressure, causing lymph to enter the renal lymphatics, or rupture of intestinal lymphatics into the renal pelvis/ureter, forming a lympho-urinary fistula. Diagnostic Tools: Urine study, culture, intravenous urogram (IVU), lymphangiography, and abdominal ultrasound. Management: Dietary changes (low-fat, protein-rich diet). Renal stone disease (Option A): While renal stones can cause urinary symptoms, they do not typically lead to chyluria or milky white urine. Tuberculosis (Option C): Although tuberculosis can cause urinary symptoms, it is not the most common cause of chyluria compared to filarial infections & also the history is not pointing towards TB. ="customMeta" data-dictid="eba212cd6616927772014f0fc1ccfd">vascularization is generally absent in pure fungal keratitis, which distinguishes it from bacterial infections where vascularization is more common.

Keratomycosis

 

Clinical Features

  • Pain & Foreign Body Sensation
  • Watering of the eye
  • Photophobia
  • Blurred Vision
  • Redness.

Examination Findings

  • Corneal Ulcer: Greyish-white, dry-looking with elevated, rolled-out margins.
  • Pigmented Ulcer: Brownish appearance, possible with dematiaceous fungi.
  • Feathery Extensions (Option A ruled out): Delicate, finger-like projections into the surrounding stroma.
  • Sterile Immune Ring (Option C ruled out): Yellow line of demarcation where fungal antigen and host antibodies meet.
  • Satellite Lesions: Multiple small lesions around the main ulcer.
  • Hypopyon: Large, non-sterile, even with a small ulcer.
  • Endothelial Plaque (Option D ruled out): Located under the stromal lesion, made of fibrin and leucocytes.
  • Corneal Vascularization: Typically absent in pure fungal ulcers.
  • Perforation: Rare but possible.

Investigations

  • Corneal Scraping: Performed under topical anaesthesia for microbiological examination.
  • Wet KOH Mount: Reveals filamentous fungi (branched, septate hyphae) or non-filamentous yeast-like fungi (Candida).
  • Gram's & Giemsa Stains: To detect fungal hyphae and inflammatory cells.
  • Culture: Sabouraud's agar medium is used for fungal culture.
  • PCR: Recommended for rapid identification of fungal pathogens.
  • Anterior Chamber Paracentesis: Considered if there is an intraocular extension.
  • Corneal Biopsy: Indicated for deep stromal abscess or when cultures are negative.
  • Confocal Microscopy: Used for identifying actual fungi within the cornea.

options.label: A
options.text: To apply direct pressure on the bleeding site

options.label: B
options.text: To reduce distal blood flow and convert arterial pressure to venous-like pressure

options.label: C
options.text: To increase uterine contractility and reduce bleeding

options.label: D
options.text: To promote rapid healing of uterine tissues

questions.answerText: To reduce distal blood flow and convert arterial pressure to venous-like pressure
questions.solution: principle of bilateral internal iliac artery ligation is to reduce blood flow to the uterus and pelvis, significantly lowering pulse pressure (85% reduction) in arteries distal to the ligation. This reduction in pressure makes the blood vessels more conducive to hemostasis through clot formation, similar to venous circulation. Considerations: Ligation of the internal iliac artery is to be done at 5cm distal to common iliac bifurcation - this avoids the posterior division branches of the internal iliac artery. Should not perforate continuous large veins, esp. Internal iliac vein. Non-absorbable sutures are used. Direct pressure on the bleeding site (Option A) is not the principle behind internal iliac artery ligation. This option refers more to methods like uterine tamponade or manual compression, which aim to directly compress the bleeding area to stop hemorrhage. Increasing uterine contractility is achieved with uterotonic agents like oxytocin, not through surgical ligation of arteries. Internal iliac artery ligation does not affect uterine muscle contraction directly. (Option C) Promoting rapid healing of uterine tissues (Option D) is not the aim of internal iliac artery ligation. The procedure focuses on reducing blood flow to control hemorrhage, not on directly promoting tissue healing. @Neet_pg_bot

principle of bilateral internal iliac artery ligation is to reduce blood flow to the uterus and pelvis, significantly lowering pulse pressure (85% reduction) in arteries distal to the ligation. This reduction in pressure makes the blood vessels more conducive to hemostasis through clot formation, similar to venous circulation.

 

Considerations:

  • Ligation of the internal iliac artery is to be done at 5cm distal to common iliac bifurcation - this avoids the posterior division branches of the internal iliac artery.
  • Should not perforate continuous large veins, esp. Internal iliac vein.
  • Non-absorbable sutures are used.

Direct pressure on the bleeding site (Option A) is not the principle behind internal iliac artery ligation. This option refers more to methods like uterine tamponade or manual compression, which aim to directly compress the bleeding area to stop hemorrhage.

 

Increasing uterine contractility is achieved with uterotonic agents like oxytocin, not through surgical ligation of arteries. Internal iliac artery ligation does not affect uterine muscle contraction directly. (Option C)

 

Promoting rapid healing of uterine tissues (Option D) is not the aim of internal iliac artery ligation. The procedure focuses on reducing blood flow to control hemorrhage, not on directly promoting tissue healing.

      • Hematogenous Spread: Typically associated with respiratory infections, endocarditis, or dental infections.
    • Symptoms include fever, confusion, seizures, focal neurological deficits and raised ICT.
    • Most common in the frontal lobe, but are also frequently found in the parietal lobe, particularly in cases of hematogenous spread.
    • Imaging:
      • CT Scan (Initial Choice): Shows hypodense oedema initially, progressing to a ring-enhancing mass as the abscess matures.
      • MRI (IOC): Identifies restricted diffusion
    • Management: (Mainstay: Surgery + Antibiotics)
      • Early Surgical Drainage: Essential for effective treatment.
      • Antibiotics: IV antibiotics are administered for approximately 6 weeks.
      • Prophylactic Anticonvulsants: Considered due to a high risk of seizures.
      • Multiple smaller abscesses: IV Antibiotics.
      • Steroids: Reduce oedema and alleviate symptoms of mass effect.

questions.stem: A 12-year-old child presents with headaches, visual disturbances, and delayed growth. An MRI of the brain reveals a 3 cm cystic mass with calcifications. The growth was found to be encapsulated and multiloculated. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 12-year-old child presents with headaches, visual disturbances, and delayed growth. An MRI of the brain reveals a 3 cm cystic mass with calcifications. The growth was found to be encapsulated and multiloculated. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: mas are benign tumours arising from vestigial remnants of the Rathke pouch. They commonly occur in the suprasellar region and often present as encapsulated and multiloculated cystic masses with calcifications. The cysts contain cholesterol-rich, thick brownish-yellow fluid (compared to machine oi). It has 2 histological variants: Adamantinomatous and papillary. The common presentations include headaches and visual disturbances like bitemporal hemianopia due to optic chiasma compression, while children present with growth retardation due to pituitary hypofunction and GH deficiency. Oligodendroglioma (Option A): Typically affects adults (30–50 years old). Commonly located in the cerebral hemispheres , not suprasellar. Calcifications can be present, but they are intra-axial and not cystic or multiloculated. Endocrine symptoms are rare . Meningioma (Option B): Rare in children; typically seen in middle-aged to older adults . Usually extra-axial , solid , may calcify but are not cystic or multiloculated. Often found incidentally unless very large. It does not cause hormonal dysfunction in children. Pituitary Adenoma(Option D): Unlikely in a child. Pituitary adenomas are rare in children. Typically, adenomas cause endocrine symptoms, but visual changes in children from adenomas are uncommon. Less likely to be calcified or multiloculated. Usually, solid tumours are not cystic. @Neet_pg_bot

d="08e2e9f18c169277718155d36ba98e">anus during bimanual traction of buttocks

 

Explanation:

 

  • Also called reflex anal dilatation (RAD), this refers to the reflexive opening of the anus when the buttocks are parted.

  • Not specific for sexual assault — it can occur in:

    • Children or adults with chronic constipation

    • Neurological conditions

    • Healthy individuals during examination (especially under stress)

  • Its presence does not confirm sodomy and is not considered reliable forensic evidence in the context of recent assault.

Therefore, it is the least supportive finding in the context of recent sodomy (within 4 hours).

Among the listed options, paradoxical anal dilatation is least likely to support recent sexual assault, especially in the absence of other corroborative signs. Its presence alone has low forensic value and can occur in non-abuse contexts.

Feature Habitual Passive Agent Non-Habitual Passive Agent
Anal sphincter tone Decreased or lax Normal or tight
Paradoxical anal dilatation Common (Option C) May be absent or mild
Perianal scars Frequently present (due to repeated trauma) Absent or rare
Radial mucosal folds Effaced or obliterated due to repeated stretching Usually well preserved
Rectal mucosa  May show signs of prolapse or eversion Normal unless recent severe trauma (Option D ruled out)
Local injury (abrasion/laceration) Usually absent (tissues adapted over time) Common after recent assault (Option A ruled out)
Pain/tenderness Often absent Typically present post-assault
Sphincter contraction on touch May be absent or weak Present (normal reflex)
Medical history May include chronic constipation or previous assaults Often no relevant history

 

  • These findings are not diagnostic in isolation and should always be interpreted in the context of history, time since assault, and forensic standards.

  • The presence of chronic changes (like loss of radial folds, laxity, and scarring) supports the possibility of habitual anal intercourse.

  • In contrast, acute traumatic signs such as abrasions, contusions, and fresh lacerations point toward non-habitual (recent) assault.

 

Dried semen around the anus (Option B):

  • Semen can dry within a few hours but still be detectable by forensic tests like:

    • Acid phosphatase test

    • PSA test

    • Sperm detection under microscope

  • Strongly supports recent penetration and ejaculation.

A 45-year-old woman with a history of chronic constipation visits her primary care physician. She has been prescribed bisacodyl, a stimulant laxative, to help with her bowel movements. The physician advises her to take the medication before bedtime.
What is the BEST explanation for prescribing bisacodyl before bedtime?

options.label: A
options.text: Bisacodyl takes 6-8 hours to reach the small bowel, thus needs to be given at bedtime for morning evacuation.

options.label: B
options.text: Bisacodyl has an associated sedative effect, thus needs to be prescribed before sleep.

options.label: C
options.text: The drug requires hydrolysis by endogenous esterases in the bowel for activation, which takes 6–10 hours on oral dose.

options.label: D
options.text: Bisacodyl mechanism of action involves the process of fermentation, which needs 6-8 hours to take place.

questions.answerText: The drug requires hydrolysis by endogenous esterases in the bowel for activation, which takes 6–10 hours on oral dose.
questions.solution: ng>Explanation: Bisacodyl and other Stimulant laxatives require hydrolysis by endogenous esterases in the bowel for activation, so the Bisacodyl effects are seen after 6–10 hours of an oral dose. However, Bisacodyl can also be given via rectal suppositories which act within 15-60 mins. Bisacodyl acts by causing low grade inflammation in small and large bowel, stimulating intestinal motility and promoting accumulation of water and electrolytes. Hence, there’s no relation with the drug reaching the colon to act. (Option A ruled out) Bisacodyl does not have any sedative or sleep inducing effect. ( Option B ruled out) Bisacodyl does not involve fermentation. It is activated by the process of hydrolysis by endogenous esterases. (Option D rule out) @Neet_pg_bot

Galeazzi fracture

Aetiology

  • It is more common in adults.
  • Three times more common than Monteggia fracture (Option C ruled out)

Mechanism

  • Fall on an outstretched hand (marked pronation of the forearm).
  • Direct blow on the dorsolateral side of the forearm

Clinical features

  • Prominence and tenderness at the distal end of the ulna (main feature).

Nausea and Vomiting Due to abdominal inflammation. Anorexia Loss of appetite. Rebound Tenderness Increased pain upon sudden release of pressure on the abdomen, indicating peritoneal irritation. Psoas Sign Pain on passive extension of the right hip, indicating irritation of the iliopsoas muscle group. Obturator Sign Pain elicited by internal rotation of the right thigh while supine, suggesting irritation of the obturator internus muscle. Dunphy's Sign Increased pain in the RLQ with coughing, indicating peritoneal irritation. Aaron's Sign Referred pain in the epigastrium upon pressure over McBurney's point. Ten Horn Sign Increased pain during gentle traction or pulling of the right testicle in male patients, suggesting an inflamed appendix close to the right spermatic cord. sign in acute appendicitis characterized by cutaneous hyperesthesia in the right lower quadrant.
  • The area is roughly triangular, bounded by lines joining the anterior superior iliac spine, umbilicus, and pubic symphysis.

    • Clinical features of appendicitis

    Symptoms

    Pain

    Initial: Vague, dull pain around the umbilicus.

    Progression: Pain localizes to the right lower quadrant (RLQ) due to parietal peritoneum involvement.

    Nausea and Vomiting

    Due to abdominal inflammation.

    Anorexia

    Loss of appetite.

    Signs

    Tenderness

    Tenderness at McBurney's point (one-third of the distance from the anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus on the right side).

    Rebound Tenderness

    Increased pain upon sudden release of pressure on the abdomen, indicating peritoneal irritation.

    Rovsing's Sign

    Positive when palpation of the left lower quadrant causes pain in the right lower quadrant, suggesting peritoneal irritation.

    Psoas Sign

    Pain on passive extension of the right hip, indicating irritation of the iliopsoas muscle group.

    Obturator Sign

    Pain elicited by internal rotation of the right thigh while supine, suggesting irritation of the obturator internus muscle.

    Dunphy's Sign

    Increased pain in the RLQ with coughing, indicating peritoneal irritation.

    Aaron's Sign

    Referred pain in the epigastrium upon pressure over McBurney's point.

    Ten Horn Sign

    Increased pain during gentle traction or pulling of the right testicle in male patients, suggesting an inflamed appendix close to the right spermatic cord.

     

    While this sign is indeed known as Sherren's triangle, it is not specific to retrocecal appendicitis (Option A). It can be present in various positions of the inflamed appendix.

     

    While Sherren's triangle is associated with appendicitis, it is neither highly specific nor does it rule out other causes of right lower quadrant pain (Option C). Other conditions like mesenteric adenitis or gynecological issues can sometimes produce similar findings

     

    The presence of Sherren's triangle does not contraindicate any specific surgical approach (Option D). The choice between open and laparoscopic appendectomy depends on various factors including surgeon preference, patient characteristics, and available resources

questions.solution: ng> The scenario with X-ray findings points towards a right Clavicular fracture, most commonly caused by a fall directly onto the shoulder . Clavicle or Collarbone : It is a long, slightly S-shaped bone located horizontally at the junction of the neck and trunk. It articulates medially with the sternum and the cartilage of the first rib and laterally with the acromion process of the scapula. Structural features: It is the only long bone that lies horizontally , does not contain a medullary cavity , and remains subcutaneous along its entire length. Ossification: It is the first bone to begin ossifying (between the fifth and sixth week of fetal development) and the last to finish ossification (around 25 years of age). It is the only long bone that ossifies from two primary centers . It primarily ossifies in the membrane, except for its medial end, which ossifies in cartilage (unlike other long bones). Mechanism of Injury: Fall on the shoulder : The most common mechanism is a fall directly onto the point of the shoulder, accounting for 91% of cases. Direct injury (Option A) : Incorrect because direct trauma (such as a blow or impact over the clavicle) is a less common mechanism than indirect force from a shoulder fall. Fall onto an outstretched hand (Option B) : Incorrect because this mechanism typically causes scaphoid fractures , distal radius fractures , or shoulder dislocations , not clavicle fractures. Fall from a height (Option D) : Incorrect because while it can result in clavicle fractures, it is not the most common cause. It usually leads to multiple injuries , and the clavicle is not selectively involved unless the person lands on their shoulder. @Neet_pg_bot

Management & Complications of urethral injuries

 

 

Anterior Urethral Injuries

Posterior Urethral Injuries

Management
  • Minor Injuries: Managed conservatively with catheterization or suprapubic catheter if severe bruising
  • Severe Injuries: Surgical intervention like primary repair, urethroplasty, or end-to-end anastomosis
  • Antibiotics: To prevent infection
  • Initial Management: Suprapubic catheterization for urinary diversion
  • Delayed Urethroplasty (Definitive management): 3-6 months post-injury after inflammation and fibrosis have subsided
  • Primary Realignment: Occasionally attempted if conditions permit
  • Endoscopic Realignment: For selected cases, though often reserved for acute management

Complications
  • Urethral stricture (risk of recurrence)
  • Erectile dysfunction (especially if injury near the penile base)
  • Urinary incontinence (less common)
  • Infection (urethritis or abscess formation)
  • Urethral stricture (most common long-term complication)
  • Urinary incontinence (due to sphincter damage)
  • Erectile dysfunction (common, due to injury near neurovascular structures)
  • Bladder neck contracture
  • Chronic pelvic syndrome

 

Immediate surgical repair (Option A) is generally not recommended due to the high risk of complications like infection and stricture formation. This approach is more suitable for anterior urethral injuries.

 

Suprapubic catheterization (Option B) is a temporary measure for diverting urine and stabilizing the patient, not a definitive treatment.

 

Long-term Foley catheterization (Option D) is also temporary and can lead to complications; definitive surgical repair is usually required.

questions.stem: Which of the following by-products from the Krebs Cycle is involved in heme synthesis?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following by-products from the Krebs Cycle is involved in heme synthesis?
questions.solution: Succinyl-CoA and glycine are precursors for δ-aminolevulinic acid (ALA), the first step in heme synthesis. In the heme synthesis, succinyl-CoA combines with glycine to form δ-aminolevulinic acid (ALA), the first step. Succinyl-CoA is replenished via anaplerotic reactions involving amino acids like Valine, Isoleucine, and Methionine , which are converted to Propionyl-CoA before forming Succinyl-CoA. Propionyl CoA from odd fatty acid breakdown enters the pathway by converting to Succinyl CoA. Citrate (Option A) is a 6-carbon molecule formed from acetyl-CoA and oxaloacetate. Citrate serves as an intermediate in the TCA cycle and plays a key role in fatty acid and cholesterol synthesis by transporting acetyl-CoA from the mitochondria to the cytoplasm. α-Ketoglutarate (Option B) is a 5-carbon molecule involved in amino acid metabolism and serves as an intermediate in the Krebs Cycle. It undergoes a Transamination Reaction to form Glutamate, which is a Reversible reaction.(α-Ketoglutarate ↔ Glutamate) Glutamate is derived from α-ketoglutarate and can be synthesized from Histidine, Proline, Arginine, and Glutamine via transamination and deamination reactions. Malate (Option D ): Malate is an intermediate in the Krebs Cycle, formed from fumarate and converted into oxaloacetate. Malate can be converted to pyruvate by Malic Enzyme, generating NADPH , which is crucial for fatty acid synthesis. It is crucial as pyruvate can yield both Acetyl CoA (Pyruvate dehydrogenase) and Oxaloacetate (Pyruvate carboxylase), enabling their entry into the Citric cycle. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
• Succinyl-CoA and glycine are precursors for δ-aminolevulinic acid (ALA), the first step in heme synthesis.
  • In the heme synthesis, succinyl-CoA combines with glycine to form δ-aminolevulinic acid (ALA), the first step.
  • Succinyl-CoA is replenished via anaplerotic reactions involving amino acids like Valine, Isoleucine, and Methionine, which are converted to Propionyl-CoA before forming Succinyl-CoA.
  • Propionyl CoA from odd fatty acid breakdown enters the pathway by converting to Succinyl CoA.

Citrate (Option A) is a 6-carbon molecule formed from acetyl-CoA and oxaloacetate. Citrate serves as an intermediate in the TCA cycle and plays a key role in fatty acid and cholesterol synthesis by transporting acetyl-CoA from the mitochondria to the cytoplasm.

α-Ketoglutarate (Option B) is a 5-carbon molecule involved in amino acid metabolism and serves as an intermediate in the Krebs Cycle.

  • It undergoes a Transamination Reaction to form Glutamate, which is a Reversible reaction.(α-Ketoglutarate ↔ Glutamate)
  • Glutamate is derived from α-ketoglutarate and can be synthesized from Histidine, Proline, Arginine, and Glutamine via transamination and deamination reactions.

Malate (Option D): Malate is an intermediate in the Krebs Cycle, formed from fumarate and converted into oxaloacetate.

  • Malate can be converted to pyruvate by Malic Enzyme, generating NADPH, which is crucial for fatty acid synthesis.
  • It is crucial as pyruvate can yield both Acetyl CoA (Pyruvate dehydrogenase) and Oxaloacetate (Pyruvate carboxylase), enabling their entry into the Citric cycle.

s against collagen VII suggest a diagnosis of epidermolysis bullosa aquisita (EBA).

Epidermolysis bullosa aquisita:

It is a subepidermal blistering disease defined by autoantibodies against type VII collagen. It has two forms:

  1. Mechanobullous variant: Skin fragility, erosions, blisters, crusts, and scars on trauma‐prone areas such as the hands, knuckles, elbows, knees, and toes
  1. Inflammatory variant: present similar to bullous pemphigoid.

HPE examination will show subepidermal blistering with immunofluorescence showing linear deposition of IgG at the dermal-epidermal junction. Patients have antibodies against collagen VII.

Pemphigoid diseases and target antigen:

Disease

Target antigens

BP 180, BP 230

Linear IgA disease

LAD1

Collagen VII

Collagen VII

BP 180, laminin 332

Dermatitis Herpetiformis

Incorrect options 

Linear IgA disease (Option A): Characterized by linear deposition of IgA at the basement membrane zone. Common in children (chronic bullous disease of childhood) but also occurs in adults. Not associated with anti-collagen VII antibodies. Typically shows “string of pearls” arrangement of blisters.

Bullous pemphigoid (Option B): Involves IgG antibodies against BP180 (collagen XVII) and BP230, not collagen VII. Causes tense subepidermal blisters, usually in the elderly. Common on trunk and extremities, less often in groin. Not associated with anti-collagen VII antibodies.

Pemphigus vulgaris (Option D): Caused by IgG antibodies against desmoglein 3 (and sometimes desmoglein 1). Leads to intraepidermal (suprabasal) blisters, which are fragile and rupture easily. Mucosal involvement is common. Not associated with collagen VII.

Cystinosis

Etiology

Mutations in the CTNS gene (Option C) (encoding the protein cystinosin, a cystine transporter) → Defect in cystinosin → Accumulation of cystine crystals in major organs (kidney, liver, eyes, brain)

Clinical Features

  • Renal: Fanconi syndrome, polyuria, polydipsia, rickets, growth failure

  • Skin/Hair: Fair skin, blond hair

  • Eyes: Photophobia, retinopathy, ↓ visual acuity

  • Other: Fever (↓ sweating), hypothyroidism, hepatosplenomegaly, delayed puberty

Diagnosis

  • Detection of cystine crystals in the cornea.
  • Confirmed by measuring increased cystine content in leukocytes.

Treatment

  • Therapy with cysteamine (converts cystine to cysteine)
  • Cysteamine eye drops for ocular involvement.

questions.solution: strong>Explanation: Mucoepidermoid carcinoma is the correct diagnosis in this scenario. Mucoepidermoid carcinoma is the most common malignant tumour of the parotid gland, particularly in adults. The slow-growing, firm, and nodular swelling in the parotid region, combined with the FNAC findings of malignancy , strongly indicates this type of carcinoma. The absence of facial nerve involvement and the slow progression further support this diagnosis, as these features are typical of low- to intermediate-grade mucoepidermoid carcinoma. High-grade carcinoma typically is locally aggressive and shows nodal metastases. Pleomorphic adenoma (Option A): This is a benign salivary gland tumour and the most common neoplasm of the parotid gland. It typically presents as a painless, mobile, and slow-growing mass. Adenoid cystic carcinoma (Option C): While adenoid cystic carcinoma is another malignant salivary gland tumour, it is more commonly associated with minor salivary glands and tends to show a propensity for perineural invasion, often leading to early facial nerve involvement. Warthin’s tumor (Option D) or Cystadenoma lymphomatosum, is a benign salivary gland tumor, commonly found in the parotid gland. It typically presents as a painless, cystic mass, often in older males. @Neet_pg_bot

Trimester Procedure Description Image 1st Manual Vacuum Aspiration (MVA) MVA is an outpatient surgical abortion procedure used up to 12 weeks of gestation. The procedure involves dilating the cervix and inserting a cannula attached to a manual vacuum aspirator or a 60-mL syringe. The cannula is used to remove retained tissue from the uterus. The approximate pressure is around -610 mmHg. Electric Vacuum Aspiration (EVA) EVA is similar to MVA. stomMeta" data-dictid="f955f012f716927771801d01e7d163">adrenal cortex, which is essential for cortisol synthesis. Therefore, it effectively decreases cortisol levels, making it suitable for patients with hypercortisolemia.

Etomidate

Mechanisms of Action
  • Depresses the reticular activating system.
  • Mimics GABA's inhibitory effects by binding to GABA A receptors, particularly the R(+) isomer.

Structure-Activity Relationships
  • Contains a carboxylated imidazole
  • The imidazole ring provides water solubility in acidic solutions and lipid solubility at physiological pH.

Pharmacokinetics

Absorption: Only available for IV use, primarily for induction of anesthesia.

Distribution: Rapid onset due to high lipid solubility; redistribution lowers plasma concentration post-awakening.

Biotransformation: Rapidly hydrolyzed by hepatic microsomal enzymes to an inactive metabolite.

Excretion: Hydrolysis products are excreted in urine.

CNS Effects
  • Induces hypnosis via GABA A receptor modulation (0.3 mg/kg).
  • Reduces cerebral blood flow and cerebral metabolic rate of oxygen without affecting MAP.
  • Decreases intracranial pressure (ICP) by 50% in patients with increased ICP.

Respiratory Effects
  • Minimal impact on ventilation; does not release histamine.
  • May cause brief hyperventilation and mild apnea, with slight PaCO2 increase.

Cardiovascular Effects
  • Minimal impact on sympathetic tone and myocardial function.
  • It may cause mild arterial blood pressure decline without significant changes in cardiac output or contractility.

Endocrine Effects
  • Inhibits 11β-hydroxylase, reducing cortisol and mineralocorticoid production, leading to adrenal suppression. 

Clinical Uses
  • Induction dose: 0.2 to 0.6 mg/kg IV.
  • Suitable for patients with cardiovascular issues and
  • Increased ICP
  • Effective in treating endogenous hypercortisolemia.

Side Effects
  • Associated with postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV),
  • Pain on injection,
  • Myoclonic movements, and
  • Hiccups.

Pre-medication with lidocaine can reduce pain; myoclonus can be lowered with midazolam or magnesium.

Novel Derivatives
  • Methoxycarbonyl etomidate (MOC): Rapidly metabolized, minimal adrenal suppression, similar hypnotic potency.
  • Carboetomidate: Reduces adrenal suppression potency, maintains hypnotic effects, minimal hemodynamic changes.
  • Methoxycarbonyl-carboetomidate: Combines benefits of etomidate without adrenal suppression, longer action duration.
  • CPMM and DMMM: Newer derivatives showing higher potency and rapid recovery post-infusion, promising in animal studies.

Propofol (Option A), Ketamine (Option B), and Thiopental (Option C) do not have specific effects on adrenal hormone synthesis and are not known to inhibit 11β-hydroxylase. They are primarily used for their anesthetic and sedative properties.

questions.solution: a" data-dictid="20b3ce06c5169277718756ee95c1e9">excision Explanation : Angular dermoid is a type of dermoid cyst that commonly occurs as a smooth, non-tender, soft swelling at the fronto-zygomatic suture. The formation of an angular dermoid is due to the sequestration of ectodermal tissue during embryonic development, which gives rise to a cyst containing dermal elements like hair follicles, sebaceous glands, and sweat glands. Angular dermoids are most often located near the lateral canthus , which is the outer corner of the eye where the upper and lower eyelids meet. They may also occur near suture lines of the skull. They are usually asymptomatic unless they become large enough to cause pressure effects on adjacent structures or become infected. ellspacing="0" style="border-collapse:collapse; width:588px">

Aspects

Terbinafine

Mechanism of action

Competitive inhibition of squalene epoxidase (Option C)

↓

Accumulation of squalene within fungal cells

↓

Inhibition of ergosterol synthesis

↓

Disruption of fungal cell membrane integrity

↓

Fungicidal action

Features

It has a high affinity for sebum and thus accumulates in sebum, stratum corneum and nails.

Uses

  • Topical: Used for treating tinea infections (ringworm) and pityriasis versicolor (fungal skin infection).
  • Oral: DOC for onychomycosis (fungal infection of the nails), tinea capitis (scalp ringworm), and extensive fungal lesions.

It is also used in oromucosal candidiasis as an alternative to fluconazole.

Side effects

Taste disturbance and rash; topical application causes dryness, itching and irritation.

Inhibition of thymidylate synthase (Option A)

  • Flucytosine (5-FC) converts into 5-fluorodeoxyuridylic acid within the fungal cell and acts as an inhibitor of thymidylate synthase.
  • It is a narrow-spectrum fungistatic agent active towards Cryptococcus neoformans and chromoblastomyces.

Inhibition of lanosterol 14-methylase (Option B)

  • Azoles inhibit fungal cytochrome P450 enzyme - lanosterol 15-methylase, which results in abnormal membrane formation.\
  • It is a broad-spectrum antifungal agent that is active against dermatophytes, candida and other deep fungal infections (except mucormycosis)

Formation of pore in ergosterol membrane (Option D)

  • Amphotericin B has lipophilic and lipophobic sides, forming micropores in the ergosterol membrane of the fungal wall.
  • It is a broad-spectrum fungicidal agent effective against Candida, Histoplasma, Sporothrix, Blastomycosis, and Leishmania.

questions.solution: ata-dictid="ee07cb1aaf16927771856285b258d9">CVP (3 cm H2O) suggests hypovolemia , which is consistent with the patient's tachycardia and hypotension. Administering a fluid bolus is the first-line treatment to increase preload and improve hemodynamics. Central Venous Pressure (CVP) Monitoring: CVP measures the pressure in the thoracic vena cava near the right atrium, reflecting right ventricular preload and overall fluid status. Measurement Method (Invasive): Central venous catheter placed in large veins (e.g., subclavian or internal jugular), connected to a pressure transducer Normal Range: 3-8 mmHg. Low CVP Causes: Hypovolemia (blood loss or dehydration). Venodilation (e.g., in septic shock). Elevated CVP Causes: Heart failure, fluid overload, valve dysfunction. Increased intrathoracic pressure (e.g., mechanical ventilation, tension pneumothorax). Clinical Use: Guides fluid resuscitation. Helps assess heart function and venous return. Vasopressors (Option A) may be required if hypotension persists after adequate fluid resuscitation, but not as the initial step. Blood transfusion (Option C) is not indicated unless there is evidence of blood loss or anemia. Increasing anesthetic depth (Option D) is inappropriate here, as the patient is likely hypovolemic. @Neet_pg_bot

Measurement Method (Invasive):

Central venous catheter placed in large veins (e.g., subclavian or internal jugular), connected to a pressure transducer

questions.answerText: Permanent lengthening of the umbilical cord
questions.solution: trong> When the placenta detaches from the uterine wall, it descends towards the birth canal, pulling on the umbilical cord and causing it to visibly lengthen outside the vagina. This is considered to be the most reliable sign of placental separation. A gush of blood from the vagina (Option B): This is often seen, especially in the Schultze method of separation, but it's not the surest sign. Some blood loss can occur before complete separation. Rising of the uterine fundus (Option C): This sign, also known as the 'rising sign', suggests placental separation but can be affected by factors like bladder fullness or uterine tone. Uterus becoming firm and globular (Option D): The uterus becoming firm and globular during the third stage of labour indicates uterine contraction and preparation for placental expulsion. It is the earliest sign of placental separation. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml: A 45-year-old woman with a diagnosis of schizophrenia has been on antipsychotic medication for over a decade. Her family has noticed that she has been experiencing involuntary movements for the past few months, including repetitive facial grimacing, lip-smacking, and jerky motions of her arms and legs. What is the drug of choice for treatment of this condition?
questions.solution: The scenario is diagnosed as medication-induced Tardive dyskinesia, for which the drug of choice is Valbenazine. Tardive dyskinesia Description A delayed effect (abnormal involuntary movements) of antipsychotics typically occurs until after 6 months of treatment. Cause Supersensitization of dopamine (D) receptors due to prolonged exposure to antipsychotic medications. Manifestations Abnormal, involuntary movements such as: Lip smacking Chewing Darting, twisting, and protrusion of the tongue (catching fly) Choreiform hand movements (playing piano) Facial grimacing Finger movements and hand clenching In Severe cases: Torticollis (twisting of neck muscles to one side) Retrocollis (neck extension) Trunk twisting Pelvic thrusting Management Prevention: Using antipsychotic medications only when indicated and in the lowest effective doses. Regular monitoring: Patients taking antipsychotics should be regularly assessed for any signs of abnormal movements. Treatment: Reducing antipsychotic drugs (or stop if possible) Switching the medication to clozapine (least EPS-causing) or atypical antipsychotics VMAT (Vesicular Monoamine Transporter type 2) receptor inhibitor: Valbenazine (drug of choice) (Option D) Tetrabenazine- Lesser efficacy, more sedation than Valbenazine (Option C ruled out) Propranolol (Option A) is a non-selective beta-blocker primarily used to treat hypertension, anxiety, and certain types of tremors. While it can help alleviate symptoms of akathisia and anxiety, it is ineffective for treating tardive dyskinesia . Clonazepam (Option B) is a benzodiazepine used to treat anxiety disorders, panic disorders, and certain types of seizures but is not effective in managing tardive dyskinesia. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
The scenario is diagnosed as medication-induced Tardive dyskinesia, for which the drug of choice is Valbenazine.

 

Tardive dyskinesia

Description

A delayed effect (abnormal involuntary movements) of antipsychotics typically occurs until after 6 months of treatment.

Cause

Supersensitization of dopamine (D) receptors due to prolonged exposure to antipsychotic medications.

Manifestations

Abnormal, involuntary movements such as:

  • Lip smacking
  • Chewing
  • Darting, twisting, and protrusion of the tongue (catching fly)
  • Choreiform hand movements (playing piano)
  • Facial grimacing
  • Finger movements and hand clenching
 

In Severe cases:

  • Torticollis (twisting of neck muscles to one side)
  • Retrocollis (neck extension)
  • Trunk twisting
  • Pelvic thrusting

Management

Prevention: Using antipsychotic medications only when indicated and in the lowest effective doses.

 

Regular monitoring: Patients taking antipsychotics should be regularly assessed for any signs of abnormal movements.

 

Treatment:

  • Reducing antipsychotic drugs (or stop if possible)
  • Switching the medication to clozapine (least EPS-causing) or atypical antipsychotics
  • VMAT (Vesicular Monoamine Transporter type 2) receptor inhibitor:
    • Valbenazine (drug of choice) (Option D)
    • Tetrabenazine- Lesser efficacy, more sedation than Valbenazine (Option C ruled out)

 

Propranolol (Option A) is a non-selective beta-blocker primarily used to treat hypertension, anxiety, and certain types of tremors. While it can help alleviate symptoms of akathisia and anxiety, it is ineffective for treating tardive dyskinesia.

 

Clonazepam (Option B) is a benzodiazepine used to treat anxiety disorders, panic disorders, and certain types of seizures but is not effective in managing tardive dyskinesia.

questions.stem: A 45 year out female presents with persistent ear discharge, hearing loss, and a feeling of fullness in the ear. Upon examination, the otolaryngologist performs an otoscopic examination, which reveals an abnormal growth in the ear canal. Which diagnostic test is most useful for assessing the extent of her condition and guiding surgical planning?
questions.stemHtml: A 45 year out female presents with persistent ear discharge, hearing loss, and a feeling of fullness in the ear. Upon examination, the otolaryngologist performs an otoscopic examination, which reveals an abnormal growth in the ear canal. Which diagnostic test is most useful for assessing the extent of her condition and guiding surgical planning?
questions.solution: l> Based on the symptoms described-persistent ear discharge, hearing loss, a feeling of fullness in the ear, and the finding of abnormal growth in the ear canal, the most probable diagnosis is a cholesteatoma. High-resolution CT (HRCT) is critical for assessing the severity of the cholesteatoma, evaluating any osseous damage, and aiding in surgical planning. HRCT provides detailed imaging of bony structures and helps identify the extent of the cholesteatoma. Investigations for cholesteatoma: Otoscopic Examination: Direct inspection of the eardrum using otoscopy, video-otoscopy, otomicroscopy, or video-telescopy. Radiological Examination: CT Scan : Primary imaging technique to assess disease severity, osseous damage, and malformations. High-resolution CT (HRCT) is often used before surgery. MRI : Provides detailed tissue distinction with different pulse sequences. Cholesteatomas typically appear hyperintense on T2WI and hypointense/isointense on T1WI. Tympanometric and Audiometric Tests: Assess hearing loss; audiometry identifies conductive deficiencies. Rinne’s and Weber's tests differentiate between conductive and sensorineural hearing loss. Cholesteatoma is diagnosed using a combination of otoscopic examination, CT, MRI, and ancillary tests like tympanometry and audiometry. Video-Otoscopy (Option A) is useful for visualizing the ear canal and eardrum directly but does not provide detailed information on the extent of disease or bony structures. Rinne Test (Option C) is an audiometric test used to differentiate between conductive and sensorineural hearing loss but does not provide information on the extent of cholesteatoma or guide surgical decisions. Diffusion-weighted MRI (Option D) helps detect recurrence or residual cholesteatoma, particularly after surgery, but HRCT is the primary imaging tool for pre-surgical assessment of the disease extent. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: strong>Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM): HCM is an autosomal dominant condition that occurs due to a mutation in the beta-myosin heavy chain . In HCM, hypertrophy can occur in any part of heart but ir occurs maximally in the interventricular septum. Due to hypertrophy of interventricular septum, left ventricle is narrowed and starts looking like a banana-shaped cavity. questions.answerText: Non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema within 6 hours of transfusion
questions.solution: TRALI is characterised by acute onset of respiratory distress and non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema occurring within 6 hours of a blood transfusion. It is caused by an immune reaction to donor antibodies or bioactive substances in the transfused blood. Characteristics: Onset: TRALI typically occurs within 6 hours of transfusion. Symptoms: Sudden onset of dyspnea (shortness of breath). Hypoxemia (low blood oxygen levels) Fever. Hypotension. Bilateral pulmonary infiltrates on a chest X-ray, indicating fluid accumulation in the lungs without cardiac cause. TACO is a transfusion reaction with respiratory distress and cardiogenic pulmonary edema within 24 hours due to circulatory fluid overload. (Option B) . questions.solutionHtml:
TRALI is characterised by acute onset of respiratory distress and non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema occurring within 6 hours of a blood transfusion. It is caused by an immune reaction to donor antibodies or bioactive substances in the transfused blood.

 

Characteristics:

  • Onset: TRALI typically occurs within 6 hours of transfusion.
  • Symptoms:
    • Sudden onset of dyspnea (shortness of breath).
    • Hypoxemia (low blood oxygen levels)
    • Fever.
    • Hypotension.
    • Bilateral pulmonary infiltrates on a chest X-ray, indicating fluid accumulation in the lungs without cardiac cause.

 

 

TACO is a transfusion reaction with respiratory distress and cardiogenic pulmonary edema within 24 hours due to circulatory fluid overload. (Option B).

 

 

Febrile non-hemolytic transfusion reactions present with acute fever and chills without respiratory distress. (Option C)

 

 

Delayed hemolytic transfusion reactions present days to weeks later with gradual jaundice and anemia. (Option D)

questions.stemHtml: A 65-year-old man with a history of chronic heart failure presents for a follow-up appointment. He has been on digoxin therapy for several years. During the consultation, the cardiologist discusses the importance of therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM) to ensure optimal digoxin levels for effective treatment. TDM is NOT done in which of the following?

options.label: A
options.text: Detect drug levels in case of poisoning levels.

options.label: B
options.text: Use of aminoglycosides in patients with renal failure.

options.label: C
options.text: Drugs with a narrow therapeutic index.

questions.solution: Correct answer: D) Drugs with irreversible action. Therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM) is the measurement of plasma drug concentration. It is expensive and is only done in: Drugs with low safety margin , e.g., Digoxin, Anticonvulsants, Antiarrhythmics, theophylline, aminoglycoside antibiotics, lithium, and tricyclic antidepressants. (Option C) If individual variations are large, e.g., Antidepressants, Lithium. Nephrotoxic drugs used in renal failure, e.g., Aminoglycoside antibiotics and vancomycin. (Option B) In case of poisoning, detect drug levels and initiate treatment. (Option A) In case of failure of response, e.g., Antimicrobials. To check patient compliance, e.g., Phenytoin. TDM is not done in Drugs whose response is easily measurable, e.g., Antihypertensives, hypoglycemics, diuretics, oral anticoagulants, and inhalational general anaesthetics. Drugs activated in the body, e.g., Levodopa. 'Hit and run drugs' (whose effect lasts much longer than the drug itself), e.g., reserpine, guanethidine, MAO inhibitors, omeprazole. Drugs with irreversible action, e.g., Organophosphate anticholinesterases, phenoxybenzamine. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Correct answer: D) Drugs with irreversible action.

Therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM) is the measurement of plasma drug concentration.

It is expensive and is only done in:

  • Drugs with low safety margin, e.g., Digoxin, Anticonvulsants, Antiarrhythmics, theophylline, aminoglycoside antibiotics, lithium, and tricyclic antidepressants. (Option C)
  • If individual variations are large, e.g., Antidepressants, Lithium.
  • Nephrotoxic drugs used in renal failure, e.g., Aminoglycoside antibiotics and vancomycin. (Option B)
  • In case of poisoning, detect drug levels and initiate treatment. (Option A)
  • In case of failure of response, e.g., Antimicrobials.
  • To check patient compliance, e.g., Phenytoin.

TDM is not done in

  • Drugs whose response is easily measurable, e.g., Antihypertensives, hypoglycemics, diuretics, oral anticoagulants, and inhalational general anaesthetics.
  • Drugs activated in the body, e.g., Levodopa.
  • 'Hit and run drugs' (whose effect lasts much longer than the drug itself), e.g., reserpine, guanethidine, MAO inhibitors, omeprazole.
  • Drugs with irreversible action, e.g., Organophosphate anticholinesterases, phenoxybenzamine.

questions.stem: Given below are a few statements regarding the receiver operating curve. Which among the following is a false statement?
questions.stemHtml: Given below are a few statements regarding the receiver operating curve. Which among the following is a false statement?

options.label: A
options.text: The best investigation is the one whose curve is most upward and left

options.label: B
options.text: The test with the minimum surface area under the cure is the most effective

options.label: C
options.text: Can be used for comparing two or more diagnostic tests

options.label: D
options.text: Can be used for deciding optimal cut-off points

questions.answerText: The test with the minimum surface area under the cure is the most effective
questions.solution: ace area under its curve is the most effective in the receiver operating curve - incorrect and is the false statement The Area Under the Curve (AUC) ranges from 0.5 to 1 . AUC = 0.5: Test is no better than chance. AUC = 1: Perfect test. A larger AUC means better diagnostic accuracy. Therefore, the test with the maximum AUC is the most effective — not the one with the minimum area. The ROC curve illustrates the performance of a diagnostic test by plotting sensitivity (true positive rate) against 1 – specificity (false positive rate) for various threshold values. Incorrect options The best investigation is the one whose curve is most upward and left (Option A): True .A curve that bows most towards the upper left corner represents a test with high sensitivity and specificity, i.e., an excellent diagnostic test. The closer the curve is to the top-left corner , the better the test's discriminative ability. Can be used for comparing two or more diagnostic tests(Option C): True . ROC curves are commonly used to compare the performance of two or more diagnostic tests. You can visually and statistically compare the AUCs of different tests to see which is superior. Can be used for deciding optimal cut-off points (Option D): True. ROC curves help in identifying the threshold value that balances sensitivity and specificity. The optimal cut-off is often selected using the Youden index (sensitivity + specificity - 1) , which maximizes test accuracy. @Neet_pg_bot

  • The ROC curve illustrates the performance of a diagnostic test by plotting sensitivity (true positive rate) against 1 – specificity (false positive rate) for various threshold values.

 

Incorrect options 

The best investigation is the one whose curve is most upward and left (Option A): True .A curve that bows most towards the upper left corner represents a test with high sensitivity and specificity, i.e., an excellent diagnostic test. The closer the curve is to the top-left corner, the better the test's discriminative ability.

Can be used for comparing two or more diagnostic tests(Option C): True. ROC curves are commonly used to compare the performance of two or more diagnostic tests. You can visually and statistically compare the AUCs of different tests to see which is superior.

Can be used for deciding optimal cut-off points (Option D): True. ROC curves help in identifying the threshold value that balances sensitivity and specificity. The optimal cut-off is often selected using the Youden index (sensitivity + specificity - 1), which maximizes test accuracy.

questions.stem: A 34 year old woman presents with severe dysmenorrhea and chronic pelvic pain despite taking NSAIDs due to endometriosis. She desires fertility preservation. On examination, tender nodules are palpable on the uterosacral ligaments, and imaging confirms endometrioma on the left ovary. Given the clinical scenario, which of the following medications is most appropriate for the initial management of this patient's endometriosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 34 year old woman presents with severe dysmenorrhea and chronic pelvic pain despite taking NSAIDs due to endometriosis. She desires fertility preservation. On examination, tender nodules are palpable on the uterosacral ligaments, and imaging confirms endometrioma on the left ovary. Given the clinical scenario, which of the following medications is most appropriate for the initial management of this patient's endometriosis?
questions.solution: lanation: The patient’s complaint of severe dysmenorrhea and chronic pelvic pain despite initial management with NSAIDs, along with nodules and endometrioma, points towards severe endometriosis. Irrespective of the size of the cyst, expectant management is done as the patient wants to conceive. GnRH agonists (such as leuprolide) are a first-line treatment for moderate to severe endometriosis. They work by inducing a hypoestrogenic state, suppressing ovarian function, and reducing symptoms such as pelvic pain and dysmenorrhea . GnRH Agonists: Administered in depots or continuous forms, such as Leuprorelin, Naferelin, and Goserelin. They cause desensitisation and downregulation of pituitary receptors, leading to endometrium atrophy. They are also referred to as medical hypophysectomy. If GnRH agonists are to be administered for more than six months, an "Add-Back" regimen is recommended, which includes low-dose estrogens and raloxifene, a selective estrogen receptor modulator. Danazol (Option B) is a synthetic androgen that suppresses ovarian function and reduces estrogen levels. It is effective in treating endometriosis-related pain but has androgenic side effects and is less commonly used due to its side effects and long-term risks. Combined oral contraceptives (Option C) are used primarily for symptom relief and menstrual cycle regulation in mild cases of endometriosis. Letrozole (Option D) decreases estrogen, leading to a loss of negative feedback on GnRH, which in turn increases FSH and LH, leading to the formation of cysts. Hence, it is combined with OCP / Progesterone and not given alone in severe cases. @Neet_pg_bot

lanation:
  • The patient’s complaint of severe dysmenorrhea and chronic pelvic pain despite initial management with NSAIDs, along with nodules and endometrioma, points towards severe endometriosis.
  • Irrespective of the size of the cyst, expectant management is done as the patient wants to conceive.
  • GnRH agonists (such as leuprolide) are a first-line treatment for moderate to severe endometriosis. They work by inducing a hypoestrogenic state, suppressing ovarian function, and reducing symptoms such as pelvic pain and dysmenorrhea.

 

GnRH Agonists:

  • Administered in depots or continuous forms, such as Leuprorelin, Naferelin, and Goserelin.
  • They cause desensitisation and downregulation of pituitary receptors, leading to endometrium atrophy. They are also referred to as medical hypophysectomy.
  • If GnRH agonists are to be administered for more than six months, an "Add-Back" regimen is recommended, which includes low-dose estrogens and raloxifene, a selective estrogen receptor modulator.

 

Danazol (Option B) is a synthetic androgen that suppresses ovarian function and reduces estrogen levels. It is effective in treating endometriosis-related pain but has androgenic side effects and is less commonly used due to its side effects and long-term risks.

 

Combined oral contraceptives (Option C) are used primarily for symptom relief and menstrual cycle regulation in mild cases of endometriosis.

 

Letrozole (Option D) decreases estrogen, leading to a loss of negative feedback on GnRH, which in turn increases FSH and LH, leading to the formation of cysts. Hence, it is combined with OCP / Progesterone and not given alone in severe cases.

questions.stem: A 15 years old female who had a tonsillectomy 16 hours ago is currently under post-op monitoring, suddenly begins to bleed from the mouth and is noted to have hypotension with tachycardia. What is the most likely cause of this bleeding?
questions.stemHtml: A 15 years old female who had a tonsillectomy 16 hours ago is currently under post-op monitoring, suddenly begins to bleed from the mouth and is noted to have hypotension with tachycardia. What is the most likely cause of this bleeding?
questions.solution: is scenario is the slipping of a ligature. During tonsillectomy, ligatures control bleeding from the tonsillar bed. If a ligature slips or becomes dislodged, it can lead to sudden bleeding, often occurring within the first 24 hours post-operatively (Reactionary hemorrhage) . This can result in hypotension and tachycardia due to blood loss. Hemorrhage is the most common complication post-tonsillectomy and is of 3 types based on the duration: Type of Hemorrhage Primary Hemorrhage Reactionary Hemorrhage Secondary Hemorrhage Duration of occurrence Immediate complication, occur at the time of surgery. Happens within first 24 hours post surgery (Immediate complication) Seen between 5th to 10th postoperative day. Causes Inadequate hemostasis or injury to the vessels (Option C) Slipping of ligature (Option D) , hypertension or the dislodging of clot. Infection (Option B) or premature separation of the membrane (Option A) Management Application of pressure, ligation or electrocoagulation of the bleeding vessels. Initially, remove the clot and apply pressure or use a vasoconstrictor. If these measures are ineffective, proceed with ligation or electrocoagulation of the bleeding vessels. Initially by Antibiotics, if bleeding persists re-exploration is done. @Neet_pg_bot
