questions.stem: A 50-year-old woman presents with confusion and lethargy. Blood tests show elevated levels of ammonia, suggesting hyperammonemia. Further tests indicate liver dysfunction. Which of the following best describes the process of oxidative deamination in amino acid metabolism?
questions.stemHtml: A 50-year-old woman presents with confusion and lethargy. Blood tests show elevated levels of ammonia, suggesting hyperammonemia. Further tests indicate liver dysfunction. Which of the following best describes the process of oxidative deamination in amino acid metabolism?

options.label: A
options.text: Removal of an amino group from an amino acid, resulting in the corresponding keto acid and ammonia.

options.label: B
options.text: Involves only transamination reactions in the cytoplasm.

options.label: C
options.text: Generates ammonia, which is directly excreted by the kidneys.

options.label: D
options.text: Predominantly occurs in the liver cytoplasm, producing glutamine.

questions.answerText: Removal of an amino group from an amino acid, resulting in the corresponding keto acid and ammonia.
questions.solution: deamination removes the alpha-amino group from an amino acid, producing a keto acid and ammonia. This reaction, catalysed by glutamate dehydrogenase in liver mitochondria, is essential for ammonia detoxification and nitrogen balance. The ammonia formed is detoxified in the form of glutamate. The ammonia generated is processed through the urea cycle for excretion. (Option C) Oxidative Deamination: Process: Removes alpha-amino group from an amino acid, producing a keto acid and ammonia. Common Amino Acid: Glutamic acid. Enzyme: Glutamate dehydrogenase ( GDH ). Transdeamination: Step 1: Transamination (all organs) in cytoplasm forms glutamate. (Option D) Step 2 (Oxidative decarboxylation): In liver mitochondria, GDH removes the amino group from glutamate, producing alpha-ketoglutarate and ammonia. (Option B) Significance: It ensures efficient ammonia disposal, funnelling ammonia into the liver for detoxification via the urea cycle. Minor deamination Pathways: Involve enzymes like L-amino acid oxidase and D-amino acid oxidase. Non-oxidative deamination targets specific amino acids, releasing ammonia. L-Amino Acid Oxidase: It deaminates L-amino acids in the kidney. It generates hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) and ammonia as by-products. H2O2, a reactive oxygen species (ROS), is broken down into O2 and H2O by catalase to mitigate damage from ROS. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
deamination removes the alpha-amino group from an amino acid, producing a keto acid and ammonia.
  • This reaction, catalysed by glutamate dehydrogenase in liver mitochondria, is essential for ammonia detoxification and nitrogen balance.
  • The ammonia formed is detoxified in the form of glutamate.
  • The ammonia generated is processed through the urea cycle for excretion. (Option C)

    •  

     

    Oxidative Deamination:

    • Process: Removes alpha-amino group from an amino acid, producing a keto acid and ammonia.
    • Common Amino Acid: Glutamic acid.
    • Enzyme: Glutamate dehydrogenase (GDH).

     

    Transdeamination:

    • Step 1: Transamination (all organs) in cytoplasm forms glutamate. (Option D)
    • Step 2 (Oxidative decarboxylation): In liver mitochondria, GDH removes the amino group from glutamate, producing alpha-ketoglutarate and ammonia. (Option B)
    • Significance: It ensures efficient ammonia disposal, funnelling ammonia into the liver for detoxification via the urea cycle.

     

    Minor deamination Pathways:

    • Involve enzymes like L-amino acid oxidase and D-amino acid oxidase.
    • Non-oxidative deamination targets specific amino acids, releasing ammonia.

     

    L-Amino Acid Oxidase:

    • It deaminates L-amino acids in the kidney.
    • It generates hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) and ammonia as by-products.
    • H2O2, a reactive oxygen species (ROS), is broken down into O2 and H2O by catalase to mitigate damage from ROS.

questions.stem: Which embryonic structure is the fascia of Denonvilliers derived from?
questions.stemHtml: Which embryonic structure is the fascia of Denonvilliers derived from?
questions.solution: loaca Explanation: The fascia of Denonvilliers , also known as the rectoprostatic fascia (males) and rectovaginal fascia (females), originates from the embryonic cloaca , which later differentiates into components of the urogenital and digestive systems. It forms a distinct layer between the prostate and the rectum. It is a continuation of the peritoneum from the pouch of Douglas (rectouterine pouch in females). In males, it separates the rectum posteriorly from the bladder and the prostate anteriorly. It does not originate from the prostate but descends from the peritoneal reflection. It is composed of connective tissue , not smooth muscle. Urogenital sinus ( Option A) is an embryonic structure that gives rise to parts of the lower urinary tract and the internal genitalia in both males and females Mesonephric duct (Option C) , also known as the Wolffian duct, contributes to developing male internal genital structures, such as the vas deferens and seminal vesicles. Paramesonephric duct (Option D) , or Müllerian duct, develops into female internal genital structures, such as the fallopian tubes, uterus, and the upper part of the vagina. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
loaca

Explanation:

The fascia of Denonvilliers, also known as the rectoprostatic fascia (males) and rectovaginal fascia (females), originates from the embryonic cloaca, which later differentiates into components of the urogenital and digestive systems. It forms a distinct layer between the prostate and the rectum.

  • It is a continuation of the peritoneum from the pouch of Douglas (rectouterine pouch in females).
  • In males, it separates the rectum posteriorly from the bladder and the prostate anteriorly.
  • It does not originate from the prostate but descends from the peritoneal reflection.
  • It is composed of connective tissue, not smooth muscle.

 

Urogenital sinus (Option A) is an embryonic structure that gives rise to parts of the lower urinary tract and the internal genitalia in both males and females

Mesonephric duct (Option C), also known as the Wolffian duct, contributes to developing male internal genital structures, such as the vas deferens and seminal vesicles.

Paramesonephric duct (Option D), or Müllerian duct, develops into female internal genital structures, such as the fallopian tubes, uterus, and the upper part of the vagina.

questions.stemHtml: A 35-year-old patient with ulcerative colitis presents with severe abdominal distension, pain, fever, and tachycardia. Abdominal X-ray shows colonic dilatation &gt;6 cm. Ultrasound show no free fluid in peritoneal cavity. What is the first-line medical management for this condition?
questions.solution: Correct answer is A: intravenous corticosteroids The first-line medical management for a patient with severe colonic dilatation (>6 cm) on X-ray in the context of ulcerative colitis is intravenous corticosteroids, typically methylprednisolone 40 to 60 mg daily. This treatment quickly reduces severe colonic inflammation and systemic toxicity. Note that our patient does not have perforation of bowel as there is no free fluid in peritoneal cavity If there is no improvement within this period, escalation to second-line medical therapies such as infliximab or cyclosporine may be tried to avoid surgery. Early surgical consultation is recommended to prepare for intervention if medical therapy fails. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml: A 28-year-old man with a history of asthma is undergoing elective surgery. He is induced with isoflurane and given succinylcholine for muscle relaxation. Within minutes, the surgical team observes that he has developed severe muscle rigidity, a rapid heart rate, and a notable increase in body temperature. questions.solution: lcholine Explanation: In this case, the diagnosis of malignant hyperthermia is typically made based on the presence of characteristic clinical signs—such as muscle rigidity, tachycardia, and hyperthermia—following exposure to certain anaesthetic agents. Both isoflurane (an inhaled anaesthetic) and succinylcholine (a depolarizing muscle relaxant) are well-known triggers for malignant hyperthermia. The combination of these agents heightens the risk of developing this serious condition, which is indicated by the rapid onset of symptoms in the patient after their administration. Triggers of Malignant Hyperthermia: Inhaled general anesthetics Ether Halothane Enflurane Isoflurane Desflurane Sevoflurane Depolarizing muscle relaxant Succinylcholine Prior exercise, even just an hour before anaesthesia induction, intensifies the severity and accelerates the onset of rigidity. Initial Indicators of Malignant Hyperthermia (MH) During Anesthesia: Muscle rigidity Masseter spasm Tachycardia Unexplained hypercarbia Increased temperature Other Features: Cyanosis, metabolic acidosis, hypertension, fever, sweating, Hyperkalemia, Hyperphosphatemia, Myoglobinemia, Myoglobinuria, Cardiac Arrest, DIC, etc. @Neet_pg_bot

Another protein-specific test to detect CSF. Secreted by the meninges and choroid plexus. Also known as prostaglandin D synthase. High sensitivity and specificity. CSF Rhinorrhea - Biochemical Tests

Glucose estimation test

Beta-2 Transferrin test

Beta trace protein test
  • Rapid but unreliable test using glucose oxidase paper.
  • Not specific for the site or side of the leak.
  • A protein unique to CSF, not found in nasal discharge.
  • Its presence is a specific and sensitive test for CSF rhinorrhea.
  • Requires only a few drops of CSF for testing.
  • Found in CSF, perilymph, and aqueous humor.
  • The best test for confirming CSF in nasal fluid, but doesn’t localize the leak.
  • Another protein-specific test to detect CSF.
  • Secreted by the meninges and choroid plexus.
  • Also known as prostaglandin D synthase.
  • High sensitivity and specificity.
  • Present in other tissues (testes, heart) and altered in conditions like renal failure and CNS diseases.
  • But, facilities to test these are not easily available. (Option D)

Glucose oxidase paper test(Option A): This test is unreliable for detecting CSF rhinorrhea due to potential false positives from other substances and false negatives if glucose levels in CSF are low or if there is active meningitis.

Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) test(Option C): LDH is a non-specific enzyme that is not suitable for diagnosing CSF rhinorrhea as it does not differentiate between CSF and other fluids in the nasal cavity.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman with a history of schizophrenia has been on antipsychotic treatment for three years. After being prescribed a new medication, she developed unusual muscle contractions in her neck and jaw within a week, resulting in difficulty controlling her head movements, which often twist to one side. Which pathway is primarily responsible for these symptoms?
questions.stemHtml: A 25-year-old woman with a history of schizophrenia has been on antipsychotic treatment for three years. After being prescribed a new medication, she developed unusual muscle contractions in her neck and jaw within a week, resulting in difficulty controlling her head movements, which often twist to one side. Which pathway is primarily responsible for these symptoms?
questions.solution: The symptoms described in this case are indicative of Acute dystonia , a type of extrapyramidal side effect often seen with antipsychotic medications. This condition occurs when there is a disruption in the nigrostriatal pathway , which is primarily responsible for motor control. Acute Dystonia: It refers to brief, sudden muscle contractions that lead to abnormal movements or postures. Clinical manifestations: Oculogyric crises (upward rolling of eyes) Tongue protrusion Trismus (jaw muscles) Torticollis (neck muscles twisting to one side) Laryngospasm Dysarthria, Dysphasia (glossopharyngeal symptoms) Dystonic postures of the limbs and trunk. Management: It can be effectively managed using anticholinergics. Parenteral (IV or IM) is for immediate treatment, while oral anticholinergics are used for prophylaxis to prevent future episodes. Drugs include Benztropine, Diphenhydramine, and Promethazine. Neural pathways: Pathway Extent Manifestations Nigrostriatal pathway (Option C) A decrease in dopamine leads to abnormal movement symptoms like tremors, rigidity, dystonias, etc. Mesolimbic pathway (Option A) An increase in dopamine levels leads to positive symptoms such as: Delusion Hallucination Mesocortical pathway (Option B) A decrease in dopamine levels leads to negative symptoms such as: Anhedonia (loss of interest) Avolition (loss of will) Affective blunting (inability to express emotions). Asociality (decrease in drive to socialise). Alogia (decrease in verbal communication). Attention deficits Apathy (lack of concern). Tuberoinfundibular pathway (Option D) A decrease in dopamine levels leads to hyperprolactinemia, which manifests as: Decreased libido (sex drive) Decreased sexual dysfunction Galactorrhea and amenorrhea (females) {{caption_text}} @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: During the active management of the third stage of labor, which intervention is recommended to prevent postpartum hemorrhage primarily due to uterine atony?
questions.stemHtml: During the active management of the third stage of labor, which intervention is recommended to prevent postpartum hemorrhage primarily due to uterine atony?

options.label: A
options.text: Immediate IV administration of 20 units of undiluted oxytocin

options.label: C
options.text: Vigorous fundal massage combined with a uterotonic agent

options.label: D
options.text: Controlled cord traction with immediate removal of the placenta

questions.answerText: Vigorous fundal massage combined with a uterotonic agent
questions.solution: 110e175">uterotonic agent Explanation: Vigorous fundal massage helps to maintain uterine tone and prevent uterine atony , a common cause of postpartum hemorrhage. Combining it with a uterotonic agent like oxytocin further enhances uterine contraction, reducing the risk of excessive bleeding. Active Management of the Third Stage of Labor (AMTSL) for PPH: Uterine Massage : Always palpate the uterine fundus after placental delivery. Vigorous fundal massage , combined with a uterotonic agent , is recommended to prevent PPH due to uterine atony. During immediate PPH, perform uterine massage while evaluating for other bleeding sources and administering uterotonic agents. Oxytocin : Recommended by WHO as a first-line prophylactic treatment for postpartum hemorrhage. Administer 20 units of oxytocin in 1,000 mL of crystalloid solution intravenously at 10 mL/min for a dose of 200 mU/min. (Option A) Never administer oxytocin as an undiluted bolus due to risks of severe hypotension or cardiac arrhythmias. Intravenous oxytocin is also a first-line treatment for uterine atony. Oxytocin 10 units can be given IM with the delivery of the anterior shoulder (Option B) Delayed Cord Clamping/Controlled Cord Traction (CCT) : If placental separation is evident, perform expression via fundal pressure or controlled cord traction. If the placenta is not separated, perform manual removal under general anesthesia. Delivery of the placenta by cord traction before placental separation especially in an atonic uterus may cause uterine inversion. (Option D) @Neet_pg_bot

110e175">uterotonic agent

 

Explanation:

Vigorous fundal massage helps to maintain uterine tone and prevent uterine atony, a common cause of postpartum hemorrhage. Combining it with a uterotonic agent like oxytocin further enhances uterine contraction, reducing the risk of excessive bleeding.

 

 

Active Management of the Third Stage of Labor (AMTSL) for PPH:

  • Uterine Massage:
    • Always palpate the uterine fundus after placental delivery.
    • Vigorous fundal massage, combined with a uterotonic agent, is recommended to prevent PPH due to uterine atony.
    • During immediate PPH, perform uterine massage while evaluating for other bleeding sources and administering uterotonic agents.
  • Oxytocin:
    • Recommended by WHO as a first-line prophylactic treatment for postpartum hemorrhage.
    • Administer 20 units of oxytocin in 1,000 mL of crystalloid solution intravenously at 10 mL/min for a dose of 200 mU/min. (Option A)
    • Never administer oxytocin as an undiluted bolus due to risks of severe hypotension or cardiac arrhythmias. 
    • Intravenous oxytocin is also a first-line treatment for uterine atony.
    • Oxytocin 10 units can be given IM with the delivery of the anterior shoulder (Option B)
  • Delayed Cord Clamping/Controlled Cord Traction (CCT):
    • If placental separation is evident, perform expression via fundal pressure or controlled cord traction.
    • If the placenta is not separated, perform manual removal under general anesthesia.
    • Delivery of the placenta by cord traction before placental separation especially in an atonic uterus may cause uterine inversion. (Option D)

This helps clinicians choose the most effective antibiotic and dosage for treatment. {{caption_text}} Image showing E-test Step Description Setup An absorbent strip with a gradient of antibiotic concentrations is placed on a culture plate inoculated with the bacterium. Process The strip releases the antibiotic, creating a gradient in the medium. An elliptical zone of inhibition forms around the strip after incubation. Determination The MIC is identified at the point where the edge of the ellipse intersects with the strip, representing the lowest concentration of the antibiotic that inhibits bacterial growth (MIC). (Option C) Advantages Allows for the simultaneous testing of multiple antibiotics on a single plate and provides a visual, precise measurement of the MIC, enhancing accuracy compared to traditional disk diffusion methods. It identifies the specific bacterium causing the infection (Option A): The E-test assesses bacterial susceptibility to antibiotics but does not identify the specific bacterium. Additional tests like culture characteristics, biochemical tests, or molecular methods are needed for bacterial identification. It determines the bacterium's resistance to all known antibiotics (Option B): The E-test measures the MIC for specific antibiotics tested, not for all known antibiotics . Multiple E-tests with different antibiotics can be performed to get a broader resistance profile, but each test is specific to one antibiotic. It allows for the immediate administration of antibiotics without further testing (Option D): While the E-test provides valuable information, it still requires incubation and interpretation time. Immediate administration of antibiotics is typically guided by clinical judgment and empirical therapy, not solely by the results of the E-test. @Neet_pg_bot

Step

Description

Setup

An absorbent strip with a gradient of antibiotic concentrations is placed on a culture plate inoculated with the bacterium.

Process

The strip releases the antibiotic, creating a gradient in the medium. An elliptical zone of inhibition forms around the strip after incubation.

Determination

The MIC is identified at the point where the edge of the ellipse intersects with the strip, representing the lowest concentration of the antibiotic that inhibits bacterial growth (MIC). (Option C)

Advantages

Allows for the simultaneous testing of multiple antibiotics on a single plate and provides a visual, precise measurement of the MIC, enhancing accuracy compared to traditional disk diffusion methods.

 

It identifies the specific bacterium causing the infection (Option A): The E-test assesses bacterial susceptibility to antibiotics but does not identify the specific bacterium. Additional tests like culture characteristics, biochemical tests, or molecular methods are needed for bacterial identification.

It determines the bacterium's resistance to all known antibiotics (Option B): The E-test measures the MIC for specific antibiotics tested, not for all known antibiotics. Multiple E-tests with different antibiotics can be performed to get a broader resistance profile, but each test is specific to one antibiotic.

It allows for the immediate administration of antibiotics without further testing (Option D): While the E-test provides valuable information, it still requires incubation and interpretation time. Osmotic Fragility Test:

  • Assesses RBC susceptibility to hemolysis in hypotonic saline.
  • Used for screening HS and thalassemia.
  • RBCs are incubated in hypotonic saline of varying osmolarities.
  • Measures hemolysis as saline enters RBCs, causing swelling and lysis.

Normal RBC Response:

  • It begins to lyse around 0.5% NaCl concentration. (Option D)
  • Maintain shape due to balance between membrane integrity and osmotic pressure.

Hereditary Spherocytosis (HS):

  • RBCs are more fragile due to reduced surface-to-volume ratio.
  • The osmotic fragility curve shifts to the right.
  • More susceptible to hemolysis at higher saline concentrations.

Thalassemia:

  • Characterized by smaller and more rigid RBCs.
  • The osmotic fragility curve shifts to the left. (Option B)
  • Lyses at lower saline concentrations compared to normal RBCs.

  • However, this test is just a screening method, and the Eosin-5-maleimide (EMA) binding test is the gold standard for diagnosing hereditary spherocytosis. (Option A)

questions.stemHtml: A 55-year-old healthcare worker with rheumatoid arthritis is started on immunosuppressive therapy. What is the most appropriate reason to perform a two-step tuberculin skin test (TST) before initiating treatment?

options.label: A
options.text: To assess the patient's baseline immunity against tuberculosis

options.label: B
options.text: To confirm a recent positive TST result

options.label: C
options.text: To differentiate between a boosted reaction and a new infection

options.label: D
options.text: To monitor the effectiveness of immunosuppressive therapy on latent tuberculosis

questions.answerText: To differentiate between a boosted reaction and a new infection
questions.solution: on: Before starting immunosuppressive therapy, a two-step tuberculin skin test is used to distinguish between a boosted reaction from prior exposure to tuberculosis and a new infection. This approach helps confirm a positive TST result, preventing unnecessary treatment for latent tuberculosis due to misinterpretation. 1st test - read within 48 to 72 hours If positive, consider the patient infected. If negative, 2nd test after 3 weeks. 2nd test - read within 48 to 72 hours - done after 3 weeks. Positive - infected Negative - uninfected To assess the patient's baseline immunity against tuberculosis(Option A): The TST does not assess "immunity" in the protective sense, but rather latent infection . Immunity would relate more to BCG vaccination or T-cell responses. To confirm a recent positive TST result(Option B): That would be a repeat single TST , not a two-step test. To monitor the effectiveness of immunosuppressive therapy on latent tuberculosis(Option D): TST is not used to monitor treatment effectiveness. Also, immunosuppression can cause false negatives in TST. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
on:

Before starting immunosuppressive therapy, a two-step tuberculin skin test  is used to distinguish between a boosted reaction from prior exposure to tuberculosis and a new infection. This approach helps confirm a positive TST result, preventing unnecessary treatment for latent tuberculosis due to misinterpretation.

  • 1st test - read within 48 to 72 hours
    • If positive, consider the patient infected.
    • If negative, 2nd test after 3 weeks.
  • 2nd test - read within 48 to 72 hours - done after 3 weeks.
    • Positive - infected
    • Negative - uninfected

  • To assess the patient's baseline immunity against tuberculosis(Option A): The TST does not assess "immunity" in the protective sense, but rather latent infection. Immunity would relate more to BCG vaccination or T-cell responses.

  •  To confirm a recent positive TST result(Option B): That would be a repeat single TST, not a two-step test.

  • To monitor the effectiveness of immunosuppressive therapy on latent tuberculosis(Option D): TST is not used to monitor treatment effectiveness. Also, immunosuppression can cause false negatives in TST.

Based on Weibel's classification of the respiratory system, which generation of airways is most likely affected in this patient?
questions.solution: Explanation: Weibel's classification of the respiratory system organizes the airways into 23 generations, starting from the trachea (Generation 0) down to the alveolar sacs (Generation 23). The terminal bronchioles are found at generation/division 16, marking the end of the conducting zone and the beginning of the respiratory zone. This level is critical as it is the last portion of the airways involved in conducting air before gas exchange begins in the respiratory bronchioles. Division number 0 to division number 16 is known as the conducting zone of the airway . Division number 1 to 10 are known as Bronchi. (Option A & B ruled out) Division numbers 11 to 16 are known as terminal bronchioles. (Option C) Division number 17 to division number 23 are responsible for gas exchange and are known as the exchange zone of alveoli. (Option D ruled out) @Neet_pg_bot

Post-thrombotic syndrome (PTS), also called postphlebitic syndrome and venous stress disorder is a medical condition that may occur as a long-term complication of deep vein thrombosis (DVT).

  • Chronic venous insufficiency patients may have superficial vein incompetence with or without perforator incompetence or having previous DVT with complete obliteration or partial recanalisation with incompetence.
  • Develop in 20% to 50% of patients after DVT.
  • Symptoms:
    • Leg pain
    • Sensation of leg heaviness, pulling or fatigue
    • Limb swelling
  • Signs:
    • Leg edema
    • Redness
    • Dusky cyanosis
    • Perimalleolar or more extensive telangiectasia
    • New varicose vein
    • Stasis hyperpigmentation
    • Lipodermatosclerosis
    • Leg ulcer

 

Venous gangrene (Option A): Presents with blackish discoloration, blebs and edema.

 

Venous ulcer (Option B): Long saphenous vein perforator incompetence is often associated with venous ulcers, typically on the medial aspect of the ankle, and is often seen in long-standing varicose veins.

Atrophic blanche (Option C): It is localized white atrophic skin surrounded by hyperpigmentation and dilated capillaries associated with varicose veins.

questions.solution: ustomMeta" data-dictid="8866b36aa016927771938ffb10b429">nitrite + sodium thiosulfate + hydroxocobalamin is the combination of choice for the management of cyanide toxicity. Haemoglobin combines with sodium nitrite to form methemoglobin, which has a higher affinity for cyanide than haemoglobin. This results in the formation of cyanmethemoglobin. But this can easily dissociate into cyanide again, thus, sodium thiosulfate is given, which will result in the formation of sodium thiocyanate which is more stable and is excreted into the urine. Hydroxocobalamine also has a very high affinity for cyanide leading to formation of cyanocobalamin, which gets excreted into the urine. Option A: Pralidoxime + atropine This combination of drugs serves as an antidote for organophosphate poisoning. Atropine is used for atropinization of all the nicotinic and muscarinic receptors thus preventing their further stimulation, while pralidoxime is used to reverse the inhibited acetylcholinesterase and reactivate the enzyme . Option C: Activated charcoal + N-acetyl cysteine This combination of drugs is used to treat acetaminophen/paracetamol poisoning. Activated charcoal binds to the unabsorbed paracetamol present in the gut which can be flushed out using a lavage, while N-acetyl cysteine serves to replenish the glutathione stores which binds to the toxic metabolite of paracetamol N -acetyl- p -benzoquinoneimine. Option D: Sodium nitrite only If only sodium nitrite is used, the cyanmethemoglobin formed will dissociate back into cyanide and methemoglobin before being excreted out of the body. @Neet_pg_bot

  • Hydroxocobalamine also has a very high affinity for cyanide leading to formation of cyanocobalamin, which gets excreted into the urine.

Option A: Pralidoxime + atropine

  • This combination of drugs serves as an antidote for organophosphate poisoning.
  • Atropine is used for atropinization of all the nicotinic and muscarinic receptors thus preventing their further stimulation, while pralidoxime is used to reverse the inhibited acetylcholinesterase and reactivate the enzyme .

Option C: Activated charcoal + N-acetyl cysteine

  • This combination of drugs is used to treat acetaminophen/paracetamol poisoning.
  • Activated charcoal binds to the unabsorbed paracetamol present in the gut which can be flushed out using a lavage, while N-acetyl cysteine serves to replenish the glutathione stores which binds to the toxic metabolite of paracetamol N-acetyl-p-benzoquinoneimine.

Option D: Sodium nitrite only

  • If only sodium nitrite is used, the cyanmethemoglobin formed will dissociate back into cyanide and methemoglobin before being excreted out of the body.

questions.solution: p> Explanation: The Ottawa Charter is the foundational document for health promotion, outlining key strategies and principles such as building healthy public policy, creating supportive environments, strengthening community action, developing personal skills, and reorienting health services. {{caption_text}} The Declaration of Alma-Ata (Option A), adopted in 1978, aimed to achieve Health for All by 2000 through Primary Health Care (PHC). questions.solutionHtml:
p>Explanation:

The Ottawa Charter is the foundational document for health promotion, outlining key strategies and principles such as building healthy public policy, creating supportive environments, strengthening community action, developing personal skills, and reorienting health services.

The Declaration of Alma-Ata (Option A), adopted in 1978, aimed to achieve Health for All by 2000 through Primary Health Care (PHC). Key points include:

  • PHC is essential, accessible, and community-based health care.
  • Recognition of health as a human right with a focus on equity.
  • Emphasis on community participation and inter-sectoral collaboration.
  • Call for global support and cooperation to strengthen health systems, especially in developing countries.

The Jakarta Declaration on Health Promotion (Option B) (1997) set a vision for health promotion in the 21st century, emphasizing that the determinants of health include peace, shelter, education, social security, social relations, food, income, women's empowerment, a stable ecosystem, sustainable resource use, social justice, human rights, and equity.

Helsinki Declaration (Option D) is primarily concerned with ethical principles for medical research involving human subjects, not health promotion strategies.

He was diagnosed with nephrogenic diabetes insipidus based on urine analysis and plasma ADH levels. He was prescribed a combination of amiloride and hydrochlorothiazide. What is the reason for the use of thiazide diuretics in nephrogenic DI?
questions.stemHtml: A patient on long-term lithium therapy visits with complaints of frequent urination and increased thirst. He was diagnosed with nephrogenic diabetes insipidus based on urine analysis and plasma ADH levels. He was prescribed a combination of amiloride and hydrochlorothiazide. What is the reason for the use of thiazide diuretics in nephrogenic DI?

options.label: A
options.text: Thiazides reduce urine output by increasing free water absorption in proximal tubules

options.label: B
options.text: Thiazides directly increase the sensitivity of the kidneys to ADH.

options.label: C
options.text: Thiazides help to increase lithium excretion, reducing its nephrotoxic effects.

options.label: D
options.text: Thiazides decrease the risk of hypokalemia when used with amiloride.

questions.answerText: Thiazides reduce urine output by increasing free water absorption in proximal tubules
questions.solution: trong>Thiazide diuretics reduce polyuria in nephrogenic diabetes insipidus by inducing mild hypovolemia . Mechanism of Action in Nephrogenic DI: Drug Mechanism Thiazide diuretics Induce mild volume depletion → ↑ proximal tubular reabsorption of water and sodium → ↓ urine output Amiloride Blocks ENaC channels in collecting ducts → ↓ lithium uptake → renal protection Lithium Causes nephrogenic DI by damaging ADH-sensitive pathways in collecting ducts Thiazides directly increase the sensitivity of the kidneys to ADH (Option B): Incorrect because nephrogenic DI is due to ADH resistance , and thiazides do not improve ADH sensitivity . Thiazides help to increase lithium excretion, reducing its nephrotoxic effects (Option C): Incorrect; thiazides actually increase lithium levels by reducing its clearance, potentially worsening toxicity . Thiazides decrease the risk of hypokalemia when used with amiloride (Option D): Incorrect because while amiloride reduces potassium loss , this is not the main reason for thiazide use in DI . @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
trong>Thiazide diuretics reduce polyuria in nephrogenic diabetes insipidus by inducing mild hypovolemia.

Mechanism of Action in Nephrogenic DI:

Drug

Mechanism

Thiazide diuretics

Induce mild volume depletion → ↑ proximal tubular reabsorption of water and sodium → ↓ urine output

Amiloride

Blocks ENaC channels in collecting ducts → ↓ lithium uptake → renal protection

Lithium

Causes nephrogenic DI by damaging ADH-sensitive pathways in collecting ducts

 

Thiazides directly increase the sensitivity of the kidneys to ADH (Option B):
Incorrect because nephrogenic DI is due to ADH resistance, and thiazides do not improve ADH sensitivity.
 

Thiazides help to increase lithium excretion, reducing its nephrotoxic effects (Option C):
Incorrect; thiazides actually increase lithium levels by reducing its clearance, potentially worsening toxicity.
 

Thiazides decrease the risk of hypokalemia when used with amiloride (Option D):
Incorrect because while amiloride reduces potassium loss, this is not the main reason for thiazide use in DI.

questions.solution: p> In mild cases of stapedial otosclerosis where hearing loss is not significantly impacting daily life, observation with regular hearing tests is the preferred initial approach. Medical Management of Otosclerosis Management is individualized based on whether the otosclerosis is stapedial (middle ear) or cochlear (inner ear), focusing on hearing loss and quality of life. For Stapedial Otosclerosis Observation & Monitoring: (Option C) Recommended for mild cases or when hearing loss is not severe. Regular audiograms track hearing loss progression. Hearing Aids: Effective for conductive hearing loss due to the fixed stapes. Non-invasive option to improve sound transmission. For Cochlear Otosclerosis Hearing Aids: May help but are less effective for severe sensorineural hearing loss. Symptom Management: Tinnitus: Managed with sound or tinnitus retraining therapy. Vertigo: May improve with hearing treatment; other therapies could be needed. Medications for otosclerosis: Treatment Mechanism Duration Benefits Sodium Fluoride (NaF) (Option D) Stabilizes hearing thresholds and vestibular symptoms. Combined with calcium carbonate and vitamin D for enhanced effect. At least 6 months Delays worsening tinnitus Reduces conductive and sensorineural hearing loss Bisphosphonates (Option B) Stabilizes hearing loss, reduces dizziness and tinnitus. At least 6 months Stabilizes hearing loss Relieves vestibular symptoms Immediate stapedectomy surgery (Option A) : Surgery is considered in more advanced or symptomatic cases. In case of bilateral otosclerosis the worse ear is operated first and a wait time of 6 months is warranted before next surgery. C/I: Positive Schwartz sign, Pregnancy, active infection, only hearing ear, flying, diving and working at height. @Neet_pg_bot

Medical Management of Otosclerosis

Management is individualized based on whether the otosclerosis is stapedial (middle ear) or cochlear (inner ear), focusing on hearing loss and quality of life.

 

For Stapedial Otosclerosis

  • Hearing Aids:

    • Non-invasive option to improve sound transmission.

 

For Cochlear Otosclerosis

  • Symptom Management:
    • Tinnitus: Managed with sound or tinnitus retraining therapy.
    • Vertigo: May improve with hearing treatment; other therapies could be needed.

Treatment

Mechanism

Duration

Benefits

At least 6 months

questions.solution: ictid="7644c201051692777194859abcd534">pancytopenia is probably due to bone marrow suppression caused by his anti-cancer drugs. Vincristine, a vinca alkaloid, specifically targets cells during the M phase (mitosis). It binds to tubulin and inhibits microtubule formation. This disruption primarily affects cells with high mitotic activity but has a preferential effect on neural tissues due to their microtubule-dependent processes and has very little effect on bone marrow cells. No follow-up needed; continue routine monitoring (Option A) : Inappropriate because follow-up is needed due to the presence of septa and calcifications. Surgical excision or ablation of the cyst (Option C) : Surgical excision is not typically indicated for Category IIF cysts given the lower risk of malignancy. The recommended management for this category includes close follow-up with imaging every 6 months for 1 year to monitor any changes.

Bosniak Classification of Renal Cysts & Management

 

Category

Description

Management

Category I

• Simple cyst, fluid density, hairline thin wall.

• No septa, calcifications, or solid components.

• No enhancement post-intravenous contrast.

CT showing a simple cyst.

• No follow-up is required.

Category II

• Cyst with some hairline thin septa, and fine calcifications.

• Uniformly high-density (<3 cm).

• No measurable enhancement.

CT showing hairline septa and fine calcifications

• No follow-up is required.

• US or CT may be sufficient for characterisation.

Category IIF

• Multiple hairline thin septa, minimal wall/septa thickening.

• Thick nodular calcifications or uniformly high-density (>3 cm).

• Malignancy Risk: ~20%

• Follow-up:

◦ Every 6 months for 1 year with CT or MRI.

◦ Followed by Imaging done annually for at least the next 5 years.

◦ May progress to Category III or IV.

Category III

• Thickened, irregular, or smooth enhancing walls/septa.

• Malignancy Risk: ~50%

CT showing thickened septa

• Treatment: Surgical excision/ablation due to high malignancy risk.

• Imaging:

◦ Contrast-enhanced triphasic CT for follow-up.

Category IV

• Same as Category III with additional soft-tissue components independent of walls/septa.

• Malignancy Risk: ~90%

CT showing thickened septa with additional soft tissue components

• Treatment: Surgical excision/ablation is recommended.

• Imaging: Same protocol as Category III for imaging with triphasic CT.


No follow-up needed; continue routine monitoring (Option A): Inappropriate because follow-up is needed due to the presence of septa and calcifications.

Surgical excision or ablation of the cyst (Option C): Surgical excision is not typically indicated for Category IIF cysts given the lower risk of malignancy.

Follow-up imaging every 6 weeks for 1 year(Option D): This is an excessively frequent follow-up schedule, making it an unrealistic and incorrect option.

questions.solution: The management of re-exposure depends on the timing and nature of previous vaccinations. 1. Re-Exposure Prophylaxis within 3 Months: If a patient who has been bitten by an animal suspected to be rabid has completed a full rabies vaccination series within the last three months. No Further Vaccination Required: The immune response from the initial series is still strong, providing sufficient protection. If necessary, only the wound should be cleaned thoroughly, and tetanus prophylaxis should be considered. 2. Re-Exposure Prophylaxis After 3 Months: Wound Care on day 0 Administration of Two Booster Doses of the rabies vaccine. Day 0: first dose. Day 3: Second dose. This booster regimen helps to reinforce the patient's immunity, ensuring continued protection against the rabies virus. Rabies Immunoglobulin (RIG): RIG is not required for patients who have previously completed a rabies vaccination series. RIG is typically reserved for those who have never been vaccinated or have incomplete vaccination histories. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
The management of re-exposure depends on the timing and nature of previous vaccinations.

1. Re-Exposure Prophylaxis within 3 Months:

If a patient who has been bitten by an animal suspected to be rabid has completed a full rabies vaccination series within the last three months.

  • No Further Vaccination Required:
    • The immune response from the initial series is still strong, providing sufficient protection.
    • If necessary, only the wound should be cleaned thoroughly, and tetanus prophylaxis should be considered.

 

2. Re-Exposure Prophylaxis After 3 Months:

  • Wound Care on day 0
  • Administration of Two Booster Doses of the rabies vaccine.
    • Day 0: first dose.
    • Day 3: Second dose.
    • This booster regimen helps to reinforce the patient's immunity, ensuring continued protection against the rabies virus.
  • Rabies Immunoglobulin (RIG):
    • RIG is not required for patients who have previously completed a rabies vaccination series.
    • RIG is typically reserved for those who have never been vaccinated or have incomplete vaccination histories.

options.label: A
options.text: Bilateral lymph node metastases are common but occurs late

options.label: B
options.text: Hoarseness is usually a late symptom

options.label: C
options.text: The most common histological type is squamous cell carcinoma

options.label: D
options.text: It may spread to the pre-epiglottic space

questions.answerText: Bilateral lymph node metastases are common but occurs late
questions.solution: The involvement of epiglottis in laryngeal carcinoma is indicative of supraglottic laryngeal carcinoma , in which nodal metastases occur early and are commonly bilateral. Supraglottic Laryngeal Carcinoma: Incidence Less frequent than glottic cancer; about 30-35% of all laryngeal cancers Site Majority on epiglottis, false cords, followed by aryepiglottic folds Vocal cord involvement Usually late; vocal cords often spared in early stages Lymphatic spread Early and often bilateral Upper and middle jugular nodes commonly involved Cancer of infrahyoid epiglottis & anterior ventricular band may extend into pre-epiglottic space (Option D) Symptoms Early: Often silent, dysphagia, throat pain Late: Hoarseness, weight loss, respiratory obstruction, halitosis (Option B) Histopathology 90-95% squamous cell carcinoma (Option C) Others include verrucous carcinoma, spindle cell carcinoma Highly anaplastic Prognosis Generally worse than glottic cancer due to: Late diagnosis High rate & early lymph node metastasis Anaplastic nature @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
The involvement of epiglottis in laryngeal carcinoma is indicative of supraglottic laryngeal carcinoma, in which nodal metastases occur early and are commonly bilateral.

Supraglottic Laryngeal Carcinoma:

Incidence

Less frequent than glottic cancer; about 30-35% of all laryngeal cancers

Site

Majority on epiglottis, false cords, followed by aryepiglottic folds

Vocal cord involvement

Usually late; vocal cords often spared in early stages

Lymphatic spread
  • Early and often bilateral
  • Upper and middle jugular nodes commonly involved
  • Cancer of infrahyoid epiglottis & anterior ventricular band may extend into pre-epiglottic space (Option D)

Symptoms
  • Early: Often silent, dysphagia, throat pain
  • Late: Hoarseness, weight loss, respiratory obstruction, halitosis (Option B)

Histopathology
  • 90-95% squamous cell carcinoma (Option C)
  • Others include verrucous carcinoma, spindle cell carcinoma
  • Highly anaplastic

Prognosis

Generally worse than glottic cancer due to:

  • Late diagnosis
  • High rate & early lymph node metastasis
  • Anaplastic nature

questions.stem: 50-year-old man presents with complaints of blood and mucus in thin ribbon like stool, tenesmus and weight loss. MRI abdomen shows bowel wall thickening in descending colon and perirectal fat thickening and enlarged lymph nodes. First differential diagnosis is?
questions.stemHtml: 50-year-old man presents with complaints of blood and mucus in thin ribbon like stool, tenesmus and weight loss. MRI abdomen shows bowel wall thickening in descending colon and perirectal fat thickening and enlarged lymph nodes. First differential diagnosis is?
questions.solution: Correct answer is A: Colorectal cancer The presence of blood and mucus in thin ribbon-like stools, along with tenesmus (feeling of incomplete evacuation) and weight loss, are classical symptoms suspicious for a colorectal malignancy. MRI findings supporting colorectal cancer include: Bowel wall thickening which represents tumour mass. Perirectal fat thickening indicative of tumour extension beyond the bowel wall. Enlarged lymph nodes, which likely represent nodal metastases Microscopic colitis is a chronic inflammatory condition of the colon that causes persistent, non-bloody watery diarrhea. There are two main types of microscopic colitis collagenous and lymphocytic colitis. Crohn’s disease can cause bowel wall thickening and lymphadenopathy but often shows skip lesions rather than continuous involvement and is usually associated with other signs such as strictures, fistulas, or creeping fat rather than primarily perirectal fat thickening @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Correct answer is A: Colorectal cancer

  • The presence of blood and mucus in thin ribbon-like stools, along with tenesmus (feeling of incomplete evacuation) and weight loss, are classical symptoms suspicious for a colorectal malignancy.
  • MRI findings supporting colorectal cancer include:
    • Bowel wall thickening which represents tumour mass.
    • Perirectal fat thickening indicative of tumour extension beyond the bowel wall.
    • Enlarged lymph nodes, which likely represent nodal metastases
  • Microscopic colitis is a chronic inflammatory condition of the colon that causes persistent, non-bloody watery diarrhea. There are two main types of microscopic colitis collagenous and lymphocytic colitis.
  • Crohn’s disease can cause bowel wall thickening and lymphadenopathy but often shows skip lesions rather than continuous involvement and is usually associated with other signs such as strictures, fistulas, or creeping fat rather than primarily perirectal fat thickening

in is one of the factors in deciding the treatment protocol.

 

Chronic wound

Definition

Any wound which persists beyond 4-12 weeks (Option A)despite conservative treatment (dressing)

Pathophysiology
  • Wounds that fail to progress through normal stages of wound healing
  • Most commonly prolonged phase is the Inflammatory phase (Option B)
  • Formation of microbial biofilms on wound

Treatment
  • Conservative treatment- Tried first, though mostly requires aggressive treatment (surgical)
  • Surgical treatment- Debridement, control of infection and inflammation
  • Surgical treatment is done when the patient suffers from intractable pain

Examples
  • Vascular ulcers (Option D)
  • Diabetic ulcers
  • Pressure sores

questions.stemHtml: An 80-year-old female patient came with complaints of gradual progressive diminution of vision for 2 years in both her eyes. She reports that over the last year, she noticed an improvement in her ability to read without glasses. The following finding is seen on slit lamp examination over the right eye and the left eye has similar opacity. Choose the most appropriate course of management for this patient.

options.label: A
options.text: Advise lifestyle modification and review after 3 months.

options.label: B
options.text: Recommend corticosteroids eye drops and reassess in 6 months.

options.label: D
options.text: Prescribe her rigid gas-permeable contact lenses.

questions.solution: gressive loss of vision along with improvement in near vision (referred to as “second sight” ), combined with characteristic slit-lamp findings, is suggestive of Nuclear Cataract, for which phacoemulsification is the treatment of choice. Management: Surgical measures: Mainstay of treatment. Cataract surgeries: ICCE (not preferred now) ECCE SICS (Small Incision Cataract Surgery) Phacoemulsification (most preferred) Followed by IOL implantation: PC-IOL (Posterior chamber-intraocular lens) is preferred. Advise lifestyle modification and review after 3 months (Option A) would not address the cataract directly and would not improve the visual acuity. Recommend corticosteroids eye drops and reassess in 6 months (Option B): The use of topical corticosteroids after cataract surgery reduces postoperative noninfectious inflammation but it is not used as the treatment for nuclear cataract. Prescribe her rigid gas-permeable contact lenses (Option D): Rigid gas-permeable contact lenses are indicated for early-stage keratoconus with astigmatism. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
gressive loss of vision along with improvement in near vision (referred to as “second sight”), combined with characteristic slit-lamp findings, is suggestive of Nuclear Cataract, for which phacoemulsification is the treatment of choice.
  • Management:
    • Surgical measures: Mainstay of treatment.
    • Cataract surgeries:
      • ICCE (not preferred now)
      • ECCE
      • SICS (Small Incision Cataract Surgery)
      • Phacoemulsification (most preferred)
    • Followed by IOL implantation: PC-IOL (Posterior chamber-intraocular lens) is preferred.

 

  • Advise lifestyle modification and review after 3 months (Option A) would not address the cataract directly and would not improve the visual acuity.
  • Recommend corticosteroids eye drops and reassess in 6 months (Option B): The use of topical corticosteroids after cataract surgery reduces postoperative noninfectious inflammation but it is not used as the treatment for nuclear cataract.
  • Prescribe her rigid gas-permeable contact lenses (Option D): Rigid gas-permeable contact lenses are indicated for early-stage keratoconus with astigmatism.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old girl with a history of recurrent urinary tract infections presents with lethargy and muscle weakness. Laboratory tests reveal a serum potassium level of 6.8 mEq/L. Which of the following is the most likely etiology of her condition?
questions.stemHtml: A 3-year-old girl with a history of recurrent urinary tract infections presents with lethargy and muscle weakness. Laboratory tests reveal a serum potassium level of 6.8 mEq/L. Which of the following is the most likely etiology of her condition?
questions.solution: e3a661b1692777197afc2ff7bca">recurrent urinary tract infections suggests the possibility of an underlying urological abnormality. Obstructive uropathy can lead to impaired renal potassium excretion, resulting in hyperkalemia. Normal serum potassium level: 3.5-5.5 meq/L. Hyperkalemia is defined as a serum potassium level above 5.5 mEq/L. HYPERKALEMIA Etiology: Decreased renal excretion (acute kidney injury, chronic kidney disease, obstructive uropathy) Transcellular shifts (acidosis, cell lysis, rhabdomyolysis) Excessive intake (rare in children with normal renal function) Pseudohyperkalemia (hemolysis during blood draw) Endocrine disorders (adrenal insufficiency, hypoaldosteronism) Clinical features: Muscle weakness Fatigue Paralysis (in severe cases) Cardiac arrhythmias Often asymptomatic in mild cases Treatment: Prevent further progression of hyperkalemia Discontinue Potassium-Containing Substances Stabilize the Myocardial Membrane To prevent cardiac arrhythmias, administer IV calcium gluconate (10% solution) at a dose of 0.5-1 mL/kg over 5-10 minutes , with continuous cardiac monitoring. If bradycardia occurs, discontinue the infusion. Enhance Potassium Uptake into Cells : Regular Insulin and Glucose : Administer 0.3 units of regular insulin per gram of glucose IV over 2 hours . Sodium Bicarbonate : Infuse 1-2 mEq/kg body weight of sodium bicarbonate IV over 20-30 minutes . Beta-Adrenergic Agonists : Use nebulized or IV beta-agonists (e.g., salbutamol, terbutaline) to drive potassium into cells. Eliminate Potassium from the Body : Sodium Polystyrene Sulfonate (Kayexalate) : Administer 1 g/kg orally or via rectal enema, with a maximum dose of 15 g, mixed in 20-30% sorbitol. Diuretics : Consider loop or thiazide diuretics if renal function is adequate. Renal Replacement Therapy : For severe hyperkalemia, especially in cases of renal impairment or tumor lysis syndrome, hemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis may be required. For Hypoaldosteronism : Administer maintenance doses of steroids and fludrocortisone. For severe hyperkalemia (K+ >7.0 mEq/L) or when ECG changes (e.g., tall peaked T waves) are present, immediate treatment is necessary, starting with IV calcium gluconate, followed by sodium bicarbonate, insulin-glucose infusion, and/or nebulized beta-agonists. In refractory cases, hemodialysis may be needed. Mild hyperkalemia (5.5-6.5 mEq/L) should be managed by stopping potassium intake, discontinuing potassium-sparing drugs, and addressing the underlying cause. Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (Option A) : While this condition can cause electrolyte imbalances, it typically results in hypokalemia due to aldosterone deficiency. It's unlikely to cause hyperkalemia. Excessive potassium intake (Option C) : This is rarely a cause of hyperkalemia in children with normal renal function. The history doesn't suggest excessive intake. Rhabdomyolysis (Option D) : While this can cause hyperkalemia due to the release of intracellular potassium, it's typically associated with a history of trauma, severe exercise, or certain medications. The clinical presentation doesn't suggest rhabdomyolysis. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
e3a661b1692777197afc2ff7bca">recurrent urinary tract infections suggests the possibility of an underlying urological abnormality.
  • Obstructive uropathy can lead to impaired renal potassium excretion, resulting in hyperkalemia.
  • Normal serum potassium level: 3.5-5.5 meq/L.
  • Hyperkalemia is defined as a serum potassium level above 5.5 mEq/L.

    •  

    HYPERKALEMIA

    Etiology:

    • Decreased renal excretion (acute kidney injury, chronic kidney disease, obstructive uropathy)
    • Transcellular shifts (acidosis, cell lysis, rhabdomyolysis)
    • Excessive intake (rare in children with normal renal function)
    • Pseudohyperkalemia (hemolysis during blood draw)
    • Endocrine disorders (adrenal insufficiency, hypoaldosteronism)

     

    Clinical features:

    • Muscle weakness
    • Fatigue
    • Paralysis (in severe cases)
    • Cardiac arrhythmias
    • Often asymptomatic in mild cases

     

    Treatment:

    Prevent further progression of hyperkalemia

    Discontinue Potassium-Containing Substances

    Stabilize the Myocardial Membrane
    • To prevent cardiac arrhythmias, administer IV calcium gluconate (10% solution) at a dose of 0.5-1 mL/kg over 5-10 minutes, with continuous cardiac monitoring.
    • If bradycardia occurs, discontinue the infusion.

    Enhance Potassium Uptake into Cells:
    • Regular Insulin and Glucose: Administer 0.3 units of regular insulin per gram of glucose IV over 2 hours.
    • Sodium Bicarbonate: Infuse 1-2 mEq/kg body weight of sodium bicarbonate IV over 20-30 minutes.
    • Beta-Adrenergic Agonists: Use nebulized or IV beta-agonists (e.g., salbutamol, terbutaline) to drive potassium into cells.

    Eliminate Potassium from the Body:
    • Sodium Polystyrene Sulfonate (Kayexalate): Administer 1 g/kg orally or via rectal enema, with a maximum dose of 15 g, mixed in 20-30% sorbitol.
    • Diuretics: Consider loop or thiazide diuretics if renal function is adequate.
    • Renal Replacement Therapy: For severe hyperkalemia, especially in cases of renal impairment or tumor lysis syndrome, hemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis may be required.
    • For Hypoaldosteronism: Administer maintenance doses of steroids and fludrocortisone.
    • For severe hyperkalemia (K+ >7.0 mEq/L) or when ECG changes (e.g., tall peaked T waves) are present, immediate treatment is necessary, starting with IV calcium gluconate, followed by sodium bicarbonate, insulin-glucose infusion, and/or nebulized beta-agonists.
    • In refractory cases, hemodialysis may be needed.
    • Mild hyperkalemia (5.5-6.5 mEq/L) should be managed by stopping potassium intake, discontinuing potassium-sparing drugs, and addressing the underlying cause.

     

    Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (Option A):

    • While this condition can cause electrolyte imbalances, it typically results in hypokalemia due to aldosterone deficiency.
    • It's unlikely to cause hyperkalemia.

     

    Excessive potassium intake (Option C):

    • This is rarely a cause of hyperkalemia in children with normal renal function.
    • The history doesn't suggest excessive intake.

     

    Rhabdomyolysis (Option D):

    • While this can cause hyperkalemia due to the release of intracellular potassium, it's typically associated with a history of trauma, severe exercise, or certain medications.
    • The clinical presentation doesn't suggest rhabdomyolysis.

Pulmonary sequestration

Definition

 

Rare congenital lung anomaly where abnormal lung tissue is detached from the normal bronchial tree and receives blood from a systemic artery, usually a branch of the aorta. (Option A ruled out)

Types

Intrapulmonary: within the visceral pleura

Extrapulmonary: outside the visceral pleura

Pathophysiology
  • Systemic Arterial Supply: Receives blood from a systemic artery (e.g., aorta) instead of the pulmonary artery. Blood returns to the right side of the heart. (Option B)
  • Extra-pulmonary type drains through IVC and
    intrapulmonary through the pulmonary veins.
  • Lack of Bronchial Connection: No connection to the bronchial tree; does not participate in gas exchange but may rupture into an airway, potentially leading to infection.
  • Collateral Ventilation: This can occur via the pores of Kohn in intrapulmonary sequestration.

Etiology

There are two theories

  • Embryological Origin
  • Acquired Lesion Theory (Recurrent infection/inflammation ➜ cystic changes and hypertrophy of the feeding artery).

Clinical features
  • Dullness to Percussion
  • Decreased Breath Sounds over the affected area
  • Crackles: Indicate possible infection (Option C ruled out)
  • Continuous or systolic murmur from turbulent blood flow

Investigations
  • Chest X-ray: Initial detection of abnormal opacity or mass. (Option D ruled out)

  • CECT: Confirms diagnosis, details size, location, and blood supply.

 
  • MR Angiography: Visualizes abnormal blood vessels.
  • Ultrasonography: Rules out other conditions and visualizes systemic artery

Treatment
  • Surgical resection: Preferred treatment to remove the abnormal tissue and preserve the systemic artery.
  • Coil sequestration: Minimally invasive alternative, blocks the feeding artery to shrink the sequestration.

Complications of sequestration
  • Pneumonia
  • Abscess Formation
  • Respiratory Distress
  • Sepsis

questions.solution: a" data-dictid="625feb7e3a1692777183aa9d923cfd">bilateral tubal blockage, a condition in which both fallopian tubes are blocked, preventing natural conception. Mechanism : IVF bypasses the fallopian tubes by directly retrieving eggs from the ovaries, fertilizing them in a lab, and transferring the embryos into the uterus. Surgical Considerations : Women with severe tubal damage may undergo bilateral salpingectomy (removal of both fallopian tubes) to improve IVF success rates by avoiding complications from dysfunctional tubes. (Option B ruled out) Success Rates: IVF success in cases of bilateral tubal blockage depends on factors like age, overall reproductive health, and egg/embryo quality. Despite these variables, IVF remains a highly effective treatment. After about 36 hours from a trigger shot or HCG injection, egg retrieval is performed using transvaginal ultrasound-guided aspiration. Fertilization: Retrieved eggs are placed in a special medium, and normal sperm is added for insemination. If sperm abnormalities are present, intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI) is used, where a single sperm is injected directly into the egg's cytoplasm. (Option C ruled out) Embryo Assessment: After fertilization, embryos are assessed and graded. Transfer usually occurs on Day 3 or Day 5. Preimplantation Genetic Testing (PGT): It’s a procedure used to detect genetic mutations, chromosomal translocations, or aneuploidy (abnormal number of chromosomes). It’s especially useful in cases of advanced maternal age, recurrent IVF failures, recurrent pregnancy loss, or unexplained infertility. (Option D) @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: In a clinical trial for a new hypertension drug, the null hypothesis states: "The new drug does not affect blood pressure." If researchers commit a Type 1 error, which of the following is true?
questions.stemHtml: In a clinical trial for a new hypertension drug, the null hypothesis states: "The new drug does not affect blood pressure." If researchers commit a Type 1 error, which of the following is true?

options.label: A
options.text: Drug lower BP, but it was concluded that it has no effect.

options.label: B
options.text: Drug has no effect, but it was concluded as it lowers BP.

options.label: C
options.text: Drug raises BP, but it was concluded that it has no effect.

options.label: D
options.text: Drug has no effect, and it was correctly concluded.

questions.answerText: Drug has no effect, but it was concluded as it lowers BP.
questions.solution: this case: Null hypothesis : The drug does not affect blood pressure. Type 1 error : Rejecting this true null hypothesis and accepting an alternative hypothesis. Key points: In a Type 1 error, the truth aligns with the null hypothesis (the drug truly has no effect). The error lies in the researchers' conclusion, which incorrectly rejects the null hypothesis. This error leads to a false claim of a significant effect when there isn't one. Criteria Type I Error Type II Error Definition Rejecting a true null hypothesis Accepting a false null hypothesis Also Known As False positive. False-negative. Implication Concluding there is an effect when there is none. Concluding there is no effect when there is one. Probability Notation Alpha (α) Beta (β) Consequences Believing a result is significant when it is not. Missing a significant result. Example Concluding a drug has an effect when it does not. Concluding a drug does not have an effect when it does. Testing Goal Minimise α to reduce the Type I error rate. Minimise β to reduce the Type II error rate. Drug lowers BP, but it was concluded that it has no effect (Option A): This would be a Type II error : failing to reject H₀ when it is false. Drug raises BP, but it was concluded that it has no effect (Option C): Again, H₀ is false (it raises BP), but we accept it — a Type II error . Drug has no effect, and it was correctly concluded (Option D): This is a correct decision , not an error at all. @Neet_pg_bot

this case:
  • Null hypothesis: The drug does not affect blood pressure.
  • Type 1 error: Rejecting this true null hypothesis and accepting an alternative hypothesis.

Key points:

  • In a Type 1 error, the truth aligns with the null hypothesis (the drug truly has no effect).
  • The error lies in the researchers' conclusion, which incorrectly rejects the null hypothesis.
  • This error leads to a false claim of a significant effect when there isn't one.

Criteria

Type I Error

Type II Error

Definition

Rejecting a true null hypothesis

Accepting a false null hypothesis

Also Known As

False positive.

False-negative.

Implication

Concluding there is an effect when there is none.

Concluding there is no effect when there is one.

Probability Notation

Alpha (α)

Beta (β)

Consequences

Believing a result is significant when it is not.

Missing a significant result.

Example

Concluding a drug has an effect when it does not.

Concluding a drug does not have an effect when it does.

Testing Goal

Minimise α to reduce the Type I error rate.

Minimise β to reduce the Type II error rate.

Drug lowers BP, but it was concluded that it has no effect (Option A): This would be a Type II error: failing to reject H₀ when it is false.

Drug raises BP, but it was concluded that it has no effect (Option C):  Again, H₀ is false (it raises BP), but we accept it — a Type II error.

Drug has no effect, and it was correctly concluded (Option D): This is a correct decision, not an error at all.

Correct answer : Option B- Long-Chain 3-Hydroxyacyl-CoA Dehydrogenase Deficiency 

  • The scenario describes a child with severe fatigue, vomiting, nonketotic hypoglycemia, and fatty liver, alongside a maternal history of acute fatty liver of pregnancy (AFLP).
  • These features are characteristic of Long-Chain 3-Hydroxyacyl-CoA Dehydrogenase Deficiency.
    • This condition affects fatty acid oxidation and can manifest in both the child and mother, particularly with AFLP during pregnancy.
  • Other deficiencies listed do not specifically present with this combination of symptoms and maternal history.

 

FATTY ACID OXIDATION DEFECTS

CONGENITAL DEFECTS

ACQUIRED DEFECTS

1. CPT-I Deficiency:

  • Site: Liver
  • Pathophysiology: Leading to decreased fatty acid oxidation and ketogenesis, which can result in hypoglycemia (Option A ruled out)
 

2. CPT-II Deficiency:

  • Site: Primarily affecting skeletal muscle and potentially the liver in severe cases
 

3. Defects in β-oxidation Enzymes: 2 types:

 
  • Long and Short-Chain 3-Hydroxyacyl-CoA Dehydrogenase Deficiency: Can cause nonketotic hypoglycemia, coma, and fatty liver. May also contribute to acute fatty liver during pregnancy
 
  • 3-Ketoacyl-CoA Thiolase and HMG-CoA Lyase Deficiency: These deficiencies not only disrupt fatty acid oxidation but also affect the breakdown of leucine, a ketogenic amino acid.

1. Carnitine Deficiency:

  • Common in preterm babies
  • Cause:
    • Inadequate biosynthesis or renal leakage.
    • Hemolysis
  • Pathophysiology:
    • Impaired fatty acid oxidation→hypoglycemia & Lipid accumulation→muscular weakness (Option D ruled out)
 

2. Jamaican Vomiting Sickness:

 
  • Cause: Consuming unripe ackee fruit containing the toxin hypoglycin,
  • Pathophysiology: This condition inhibits medium- and short-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase, leading to hypoglycemia (Option C ruled out)

CLINICAL FEATURES
  • Hypoglycemia
  • Nonketotic Hypoglycemia
  • Lipid Accumulation
  • Dicarboxylic Aciduria
    • Marked by the excretion of C6—C10 ω-dicarboxylic acids and non-ketotic hypoglycemia
    • It arises from a lack of mitochondrial medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase.
  • Muscular Weakness due to the buildup of lipids in muscles
  • Coma
  • Fatty Liver
  • Acute Fatty Liver of Pregnancy: Due to Long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency indicating a potential role of hormonal changes influencing enzyme activity.
  • Neurological Symptoms: Defects impacting fatty acid oxidation, especially those also affecting the breakdown of leucine.

 

Differential Diagnosis:

  1. DKA (Benedict+, Rothera+): This would present with high blood glucose and elevated ketone bodies, which is not the case here.
  2. Starvation ketosis (Benedict-, Rothera+): This can also cause non-ketotic hypoglycemia, but without the fatty liver findings.
  3. Maple Syrup Urine Disease (MSUD): This amino acid disorder can impact fatty acid oxidation and cause hypoglycemia, but would likely present with a different pattern of symptoms.
  4. Type 1 Glycogen Storage Disease: This can also lead to fasting hypoglycemia, but would not typically involve fatty liver changes
